description: Optimize a surface mount technology assembly line from solder paste printing through reflow, using process capability data to drive parameter selection, SPC monitoring, and defect root cause analysis at each stage.

steps.description: Select solder paste alloy, particle size classification, and flux chemistry from board design constraints and process requirements.

inputs.name: smallest-component-pitch
inputs.desc: Finest pitch on the board in mm (e.g. 0.3mm for 01005, 0.4mm for 0201, 0.5mm for QFP)

inputs.name: board-finish-type
inputs.desc: Surface finish (HASL, ENIG, OSP, immersion silver, immersion tin) affecting wettability

inputs.name: reflow-atmosphere
inputs.desc: Air or nitrogen reflow environment

inputs.name: alloy-requirements
inputs.desc: Lead-free or tin-lead requirement, any customer or regulatory constraints

outputs.name: paste-alloy-selection
outputs.desc: Selected alloy (SAC305, SAC105, SN100C, SnPb) with melting point and wetting characteristics

outputs.name: particle-size-class
outputs.desc: IPC type classification (Type 3 through Type 6) matched to aperture size and area ratio

outputs.name: flux-chemistry-selection
outputs.desc: Flux type (no-clean ROL0/ROL1, water-soluble ORH1, rosin) with activity level rationale

outputs.name: paste-handling-requirements
outputs.desc: Storage temperature, warm-up time, stencil life, and working life constraints

process: Map the smallest aperture size from the finest pitch component. For 0.4mm pitch QFP, aperture width is approximately 0.2mm. For micro-BGA at 0.3mm pitch, apertures may be 0.15mm diameter.

Calculate the area ratio for the smallest aperture: area ratio = aperture area / (aperture perimeter x stencil thickness). Target area ratio above 0.66 for reliable paste release. If below 0.66 with Type 3 paste, step to Type 4 (20-38 micron) or Type 5 (15-25 micron).

Select alloy based on reliability and process requirements. SAC305 (Sn96.5/Ag3.0/Cu0.5) at 217-220C liquidus is the default lead-free. SAC105 at lower silver content reduces cost but has lower fatigue life. SN100C (Sn/Cu/Ni/Ge) for wave-compatible processes. SnPb (Sn63/Pb37) at 183C liquidus where exemptions apply.

Match flux chemistry to board finish and cleaning capability. No-clean ROL0 for ENIG/OSP with no post-reflow cleaning. Water-soluble ORH1 for HASL or oxidized surfaces when aqueous cleaning is available. Higher activity flux compensates for poor wettability but requires cleaning.

Document handling constraints: refrigerated storage at 0-10C, 4-hour minimum warm-up to room temperature before opening, 8-hour stencil life for no-clean, 24-hour stencil life for water-soluble. These parameters become SPC control points.

steps.description: Design the solder paste stencil with aperture geometry modifications, foil thickness selection, and area ratio optimization for each component type on the board.

inputs.name: paste-alloy-selection
inputs.desc: Selected alloy and its rheological properties

inputs.name: particle-size-class
inputs.desc: Paste particle size classification

inputs.name: smallest-component-pitch
inputs.desc: Finest pitch on the board

inputs.name: board-component-list
inputs.desc: Component types and their pad geometries (QFP, BGA, 0201, 0402, connectors)

outputs.name: stencil-thickness
outputs.desc: Foil thickness in mm with rationale from area ratio analysis

outputs.name: aperture-modification-table
outputs.desc: Per-component aperture geometry: size reduction percentage, shape modifications (home plate, inverted home plate, rounded corners)

outputs.name: step-stencil-requirements
outputs.desc: Whether step-up or step-down regions are needed and their locations

outputs.name: stencil-material-selection
outputs.desc: Laser-cut stainless steel vs electroformed nickel selection with wall smoothness requirements

process: Start with the finest pitch component to set the base stencil thickness. For 0.4mm pitch QFP with 0.2mm aperture width, area ratio = (0.2 x L) / (2 x (0.2 + L) x t) where t is thickness. At 0.1mm (4mil) thickness, check that area ratio exceeds 0.66.

Check area ratio for every component type at the chosen thickness. Large pads (connectors, power components) may need increased volume. If the ratio between smallest and largest pad deposit requirements exceeds what one thickness can serve, specify a step stencil.

Apply aperture modifications by component type. Reduce QFP apertures by 10-15% on width to prevent bridging. Use home-plate shape for gull-wing leads to center the deposit. Round aperture corners with radius equal to stencil thickness for better paste release. For BGA, use 1:1 or slight reduction of pad-to-aperture ratio.

For 0201 and 01005 components, specify aperture elongation (aspect ratio 1.5:1) oriented in the print direction to increase deposit volume while maintaining area ratio. These components are most sensitive to insufficient paste volume causing opens.

Select stencil material. Electroformed nickel for pitches below 0.4mm due to trapezoidal aperture walls (wider at board side) that improve paste release. Laser-cut stainless steel with electropolish for standard pitches. Nano-coating on aperture walls reduces paste adhesion.
Document the aperture table as a manufacturing specification. Include the nominal paste volume target per pad in nanoliters for SPI correlation.

steps.description: Configure solder paste printer parameters and establish the process window through designed experiments on print speed, pressure, separation speed, and snap-off distance.

inputs.name: stencil-thickness
inputs.desc: Foil thickness selected

inputs.name: stencil-material-selection
inputs.desc: Material and coating of stencil

inputs.name: paste-alloy-selection
inputs.desc: Paste alloy and rheology

inputs.name: particle-size-class
inputs.desc: Particle size classification

outputs.name: print-speed-range
outputs.desc: Qualified print speed range in mm/s with transfer efficiency data

outputs.name: squeegee-pressure
outputs.desc: Pressure setting in N/mm or kg with clean wipe rationale

outputs.name: separation-parameters
outputs.desc: Separation speed and distance settings for paste release quality

outputs.name: print-process-window
outputs.desc: DOE results showing the interaction between speed, pressure, and separation on volume and height consistency

process: Set initial squeegee pressure to achieve clean stencil wipe without paste scavenging from apertures. Start at 0.3-0.5 N/mm of squeegee length. Inspect the stencil underside after printing. Paste bleeding under the stencil indicates excess pressure or insufficient snap-off.

Run a print speed DOE from 20mm/s to 150mm/s in 25mm/s increments. At each speed, measure paste volume on 10+ pads across the board using SPI. Plot transfer efficiency (actual volume / theoretical volume) vs speed. Transfer efficiency should be 80-120%. Identify the speed at which efficiency drops below 80%.

Set separation speed and distance. Fast separation (>3mm/s) causes dog-ears and inconsistent deposits on fine pitch. Slow separation (<0.5mm/s) increases cycle time. Start at 1mm/s with 2mm separation distance. For fine pitch (<0.5mm), use two-stage separation: slow initial (0.3mm/s for first 0.5mm) then fast.

Run a full factorial DOE with speed (3 levels), pressure (3 levels), and separation speed (3 levels) on a test vehicle. Measure paste volume, height, area, and offset on the smallest pitch component. Use response surface methodology to find the center of the process window.

Establish under-stencil cleaning frequency. Wet-dry-vacuum every 3-5 prints for fine pitch. Monitor SPI volume trending to detect cleaning degradation. Increase cleaning frequency if volume Cpk drops below 1.33.
Lock the process parameters as the standard operating procedure. Set SPI volume limits at +/-50% of nominal for alarm and +/-30% for process adjustment triggers.

steps.description: Verify and optimize pick-and-place machine accuracy, repeatability, and throughput for the specific board design through capability studies and feeder optimization.

inputs.name: board-component-list
inputs.desc: Component types, package sizes, and quantities

inputs.name: print-process-window
inputs.desc: Paste deposit accuracy data informing placement tolerance budget

outputs.name: placement-accuracy-data
outputs.desc: Cpk for X, Y, and theta placement accuracy per component type

outputs.name: feeder-optimization
outputs.desc: Feeder assignment, nozzle selection, and line balance between placement heads

outputs.name: placement-defect-rate
outputs.desc: Expected placement defect rate (missing, shifted, rotated, wrong part) from capability data

outputs.name: machine-program-validation
outputs.desc: First article placement verification results and program corrections

process: Run a machine capability study: place 30+ boards and measure XY offset and rotation for each component type using post-placement AOI or offline measurement system. Calculate Cpk for each axis. Target Cpk > 1.67 for fine pitch, > 1.33 for standard pitch.

Verify nozzle-to-component matching. Each nozzle size has a pickup range. Map nozzle types to component body sizes. Verify vacuum level for each nozzle (insufficient vacuum causes drops, excess vacuum damages fragile components like MLCC).

Optimize feeder assignment for throughput. Group components by nozzle type to minimize nozzle changes. Balance placement count across heads. Place fine-pitch components on the most accurate head. Use simultaneous pickup where feeder spacing matches head spacing.

Validate the component centroid and rotation in the machine program against the CAD data. Run a first article with no paste (dry run) and measure all placements. Correct any systematic offset before production.

Set placement force limits. 0201 and 01005 components are sensitive to placement force pushing paste out from under the part. Typical placement force is 1-3N for chip components, 3-10N for QFP/BGA. Too high causes solder balling; too low causes insufficient contact with paste.

steps.description: Develop the baseline reflow profile from component thermal requirements, board thermal mass distribution, and solder paste specifications.

inputs.name: paste-alloy-selection
inputs.desc: Alloy liquidus temperature and reflow window

inputs.name: board-component-list
inputs.desc: Components with temperature ratings and moisture sensitivity levels

inputs.name: smallest-component-pitch
inputs.desc: Finest pitch affecting thermal uniformity requirements

outputs.name: reflow-profile-specification
outputs.desc: Zone temperatures, belt speed, peak temperature range, time above liquidus, thermal delta specification

outputs.name: thermocouple-placement-map
outputs.desc: TC attachment locations covering thermal extremes on the board

outputs.name: profile-compliance-data
outputs.desc: Measured profile at each TC location vs specification limits

outputs.name: thermal-delta-measurement
outputs.desc: Maximum temperature difference across the board at peak and during ramp

process: Identify the thermal constraints. The coldest joint must exceed liquidus + 10C (227C minimum for SAC305). The hottest component must stay below its maximum rating (typically 260C for 10 seconds for most SMD components). Moisture-sensitive components (MSL 3 and above) have specific time-temperature limits per J-STD-020.

Attach thermocouples to thermal extremes: the coldest point (typically a large ground pad or BGA center), the hottest point (typically a small component near board edge), and two intermediate locations. Use high-temperature solder or Kapton tape with thermal grease for consistent attachment.

Select profile type. Ramp-soak-spike for boards with high thermal delta (>15C between coldest and hottest). Linear ramp-to-peak for boards with low thermal delta (<10C) and no large thermal masses. Soak zone (150-200C for 60-120s) reduces delta by allowing cold regions to catch up.

Set zone temperatures starting from paste vendor guidelines. Preheat ramp rate 1-3C/s (faster causes paste spattering from volatile release). Soak at 150-200C. Ramp to peak at 1-3C/s. Peak temperature 235-245C for SAC305 with minimum 40s above liquidus (217C) and maximum 90s. Cooling rate 2-4C/s (faster improves joint microstructure but risks thermal shock).

Measure thermal delta at peak temperature. Specification is typically 10C maximum for fine pitch (<0.5mm) and 15C for standard assembly. If delta exceeds specification, adjust soak time, zone temperatures, or belt speed. Consider board support or edge rails to manage warpage.
Document the qualified profile as the manufacturing standard. Specify the acceptable range for each parameter (peak temperature +/-5C, time above liquidus +/-10s, ramp rate +/-0.5C/s).

steps.description: Execute a systematic first article inspection comparing the assembled board against design intent across all process stages, generating the acceptance baseline for production.

inputs.name: reflow-profile-specification
inputs.desc: Qualified reflow parameters

inputs.name: placement-accuracy-data
inputs.desc: Machine capability data

inputs.name: print-process-window
inputs.desc: Qualified print parameters

inputs.name: stencil-thickness
inputs.desc: Stencil specification

outputs.name: fai-report
outputs.desc: First article inspection results with pass/fail per characteristic and corrective actions for failures

outputs.name: ipc-class-compliance
outputs.desc: Classification of all solder joints per IPC-A-610 criteria at the required class level

outputs.name: process-deviations
outputs.desc: Any deviations from the standard process required for this specific product

outputs.name: production-release-status
outputs.desc: Go/no-go decision with supporting data for production release

process: Inspect paste deposits on the first board via SPI before placement. Verify volume, height, area, and offset are within the qualified process window. Confirm no bridging, insufficient, or missing deposits. This is the first gate before committing components.

After placement (before reflow), inspect for placement accuracy, missing components, wrong components, polarity, and tombstone risk (paste deposit asymmetry). On the first article, visually inspect 100% of placements against the BOM and centroid data.

After reflow, perform visual inspection per IPC-A-610 at the customer-specified class level (Class 2 for commercial, Class 3 for high-reliability). Document solder joint condition for each component type: fillet formation, wetting, voiding (X-ray for BGA), bridging, solder balls, cold joints.

For BGA and bottom-terminated components, perform X-ray inspection. Check for head-in-pillow, voiding (target <25% void area per joint for Class 3), bridging, missing balls, and pad cratering. These defects are invisible to optical inspection.

Cross-section representative solder joints (destructive) if required by the product specification or if the process is new. Measure intermetallic thickness (target 1-3 microns for fresh joints), void content, and joint geometry.

Compile the FAI report with measurements, images, and pass/fail determinations. Identify any corrective actions needed before production release. The FAI package becomes the reference standard for ongoing production inspection.

steps.description: Establish statistical process control monitoring points across the SMT line with control chart selection, sampling strategy, and out-of-control response procedures.

inputs.name: print-process-window
inputs.desc: Qualified print parameters and SPI data

inputs.name: placement-accuracy-data
inputs.desc: Machine capability data

inputs.name: reflow-profile-specification
inputs.desc: Qualified reflow parameters

inputs.name: fai-report
inputs.desc: Baseline quality data from first article

outputs.name: spc-control-plan
outputs.desc: Control chart type, measurement points, sampling frequency, and control limits for each process stage

outputs.name: reaction-plan
outputs.desc: Out-of-control action procedures (OCAP) for each chart alarm type

outputs.name: capability-targets
outputs.desc: Cpk targets and measurement system analysis requirements for each SPC point

outputs.name: spc-review-schedule
outputs.desc: Periodic review frequency for control limit recalculation and capability assessment

process: At the print station, monitor paste volume via SPI. Use X-bar and R charts on volume for 5 critical pads (finest pitch, largest pad, BGA, and two intermediate). Sample every board or every Nth board depending on volume. Set control limits from the first 25 subgroups of production data, not from the DOE data.

At the placement station, monitor placement offset using post-placement AOI or SPI delta measurement. Use individuals (I-MR) charts for X and Y offset of the finest pitch component. Offset trending indicates machine calibration drift.

At the reflow station, monitor profile parameters from the in-line profiler (if equipped) or periodic board-level profiling. Track peak temperature, time above liquidus, and thermal delta on a run chart with specification limits. Profile should be re-verified weekly, after belt speed changes, and after maintenance.

At post-reflow AOI, monitor defect rates using p-charts (fraction defective) or u-charts (defects per unit) depending on board complexity. Stratify defects by type (bridge, insufficient, missing, tombstone, solder ball) for Pareto analysis. A shift in any defect type triggers investigation.

Perform measurement system analysis (MSA) for each SPC measurement point. Gage R&R for SPI volume should show <10% of tolerance consumed by measurement variation. AOI false call rate should be <500ppm to maintain operator trust in the inspection system.
Set the review schedule: daily review of control charts by process engineering, weekly Cpk calculation, monthly control limit recalculation, quarterly measurement system re-verification.

steps.description: Diagnose the root cause of SMT defects by mapping defect types to their originating process stage, using physical evidence and process data correlation.

inputs.name: spc-control-plan
inputs.desc: Active SPC data from each process stage

inputs.name: fai-report
inputs.desc: Baseline quality data

inputs.name: ipc-class-compliance
inputs.desc: Inspection criteria in use

outputs.name: defect-cause-map
outputs.desc: Each defect type mapped to its most likely process stage origin with diagnostic evidence

outputs.name: corrective-action-matrix
outputs.desc: Corrective actions for each defect type organized by process stage

outputs.name: process-improvement-priorities
outputs.desc: Prioritized list of process improvements from defect Pareto and occurrence data

process: Bridging: if between adjacent pads on fine pitch, root cause is paste (excess volume, slump) or stencil (aperture too large, under-stencil bleed). If between non-adjacent pads, root cause is solder balling during reflow or contamination. Check SPI data at the bridged location to differentiate.

Tombstoning: caused by unequal wetting forces during reflow. Originating causes include asymmetric paste deposits (print stage), component placement offset shifting the deposit balance (placement stage), or unequal pad thermal mass causing one end to wet before the other (design/reflow). Check SPI for paste volume ratio between the two pads.

Head-in-pillow on BGA: caused by board or component warpage during reflow separating the paste deposit from the ball at the moment of coalescence. Worst at center of large BGA packages. Not visible optically; detected by X-ray showing a smooth separation line. Mitigation is vapor-phase reflow, nitrogen atmosphere, or reflow profile optimization to reduce peak warpage.

Voiding: small voids (<15% area) are inherent in reflow process from flux volatile entrapment. Excessive voiding indicates insufficient flux activation temperature, too-fast ramp through the volatile release window, or contaminated pads. Vacuum reflow reduces voiding for power components where thermal performance requires <5% void area.

Insufficient solder (non-wetting): caused by insufficient paste volume (print stage), oxidized pads (storage/handling), or insufficient reflow temperature/time at the joint. Differentiate by checking SPI volume data and comparing the peak temperature at the defective joint to the profile specification.

Solder balls: small balls (<75um) near component are typically from paste spattering during reflow preheat (ramp rate too fast, paste not conditioned). Larger balls between pads indicate paste on solder mask from print misalignment or stencil damage. Mid-chip solder balls on passives are from paste under the component body.

Compile the defect-cause map and prioritize corrective actions by defect frequency multiplied by severity. The highest priority actions address the defect type contributing the most to scrap or rework cost.

description: Design and qualify a reflow soldering profile from thermal profiling methodology through zone-by-zone optimization, accounting for component thermal limits, board thermal mass variation, and atmosphere effects.

steps.description: Prepare a thermal profiling board with thermocouple placement strategy based on board thermal topology and component sensitivity.

inputs.name: board-assembly-drawing
inputs.desc: Assembly drawing showing component locations, copper distribution, and board dimensions

inputs.name: component-thermal-ratings
inputs.desc: Maximum temperature ratings and moisture sensitivity levels for all component types

inputs.name: solder-alloy-liquidus
inputs.desc: Liquidus temperature of the solder alloy in use

outputs.name: tc-placement-map
outputs.desc: Thermocouple locations with rationale for each placement targeting thermal extremes

outputs.name: tc-attachment-method
outputs.desc: Attachment method per location (high-temp solder, Kapton tape, epoxy) with accuracy implications

outputs.name: profiler-board-specification
outputs.desc: Requirements for the profiling board: production board with components or bare board, thermocouple routing

process: Identify thermal extremes on the board. The coldest point is typically the center of the largest BGA (thermal mass of the package and solder balls acts as a heat sink), a large ground plane area with heavy copper pour, or a connector with high thermal mass. The hottest point is typically a small component near the board edge or a region with minimal copper.

Place thermocouples at minimum 4 locations: coldest point (to verify minimum peak temperature), hottest point (to verify maximum temperature limit), and two intermediate points to characterize the thermal gradient across the board. For double-sided reflow, include top and bottom measurements.

Select thermocouple type. Type K (chromel-alumel) is standard for reflow profiling: range -200 to 1250C, accuracy +/-2.2C. Use 36AWG (0.13mm) wire to minimize thermal mass of the TC itself affecting the measurement. Smaller wire responds faster but is more fragile.

Attach thermocouples using high-temperature solder (bismuth-tin at 280C+ liquidus) for joints that must reach reflow temperature. Apply a small dot of solder to the pad, then solder the TC bead to it. For component body temperature, use Kapton tape with a small amount of thermal grease between TC and component.

Route thermocouple wires to minimize interference with the reflow process. Tape wires flat to the board surface along existing component rows. Exit the board from the trailing edge (opposite to oven entry). Ensure wires do not cast thermal shadows on nearby components.

steps.description: Configure reflow oven zones to achieve the target profile shape, mapping each zone to its function in the thermal sequence and setting initial temperatures from alloy requirements.

inputs.name: tc-placement-map
inputs.desc: Thermocouple locations on the profiling board

inputs.name: solder-alloy-liquidus
inputs.desc: Liquidus temperature

inputs.name: component-thermal-ratings
inputs.desc: Temperature limits for all components

outputs.name: zone-temperature-settings
outputs.desc: Temperature setpoint for each oven zone with its function (preheat, soak, ramp, peak, cooling)

outputs.name: belt-speed-initial
outputs.desc: Conveyor belt speed setting with the resulting total time in oven

outputs.name: profile-type-selection
outputs.desc: Ramp-soak-spike or ramp-to-peak selection with rationale

process: Determine the number of heating zones available. A typical production oven has 8-12 heating zones and 2-4 cooling zones. More zones provide finer profile control. Map the zones to profile regions: zones 1-3 for preheat (25C to 150C), zones 4-6 for soak (150-200C), zones 7-9 for ramp-to-peak, zones 10-12 for peak temperature.

Select the profile type. Ramp-soak-spike: use when thermal delta exceeds 15C, when boards have large thermal mass variation, or when paste vendor recommends a soak for flux activation. The soak zone allows the coldest regions to approach the hottest regions before the rapid ramp to peak. Ramp-to-peak (tent profile): use when thermal delta is low (<10C) and components are not moisture-sensitive.

Set initial zone temperatures. Preheat zones: ramp at 1-2C/s, set zone temperature 50-80C above the desired board temperature at that zone exit. Soak zones: set at 180-200C for a soak plateau of 150-200C at the board. Peak zones: set at 260-280C for SAC305 to achieve 235-245C at the board surface (the zone must be significantly hotter than the desired board temperature).

Set belt speed. Start with the paste vendor's recommended total time in oven (typically 4-6 minutes for a ramp-soak-spike profile). Belt speed = oven heated length / total time. For a 3-meter heated length and 5-minute target: 600mm/min = 10mm/s.

For cooling zones, set cooling rate of 2-4C/s. Faster cooling produces finer grain structure and better fatigue life in SAC alloys but risks thermal shock on ceramic components. Slower cooling produces coarser but more ductile microstructure. Forced nitrogen cooling provides faster, more controlled cooling than forced air.

steps.description: Iteratively adjust zone temperatures and belt speed to bring all thermocouple readings within specification, minimizing thermal delta while meeting time-temperature requirements.

inputs.name: zone-temperature-settings
inputs.desc: Initial zone settings

inputs.name: belt-speed-initial
inputs.desc: Starting belt speed

inputs.name: tc-placement-map
inputs.desc: TC locations for measurement

inputs.name: solder-alloy-liquidus
inputs.desc: Liquidus temperature for TAL calculation

outputs.name: optimized-profile
outputs.desc: Final zone temperatures and belt speed with measured profile at each TC location

outputs.name: thermal-delta-at-peak
outputs.desc: Measured temperature difference between coldest and hottest TC at peak reflow

outputs.name: time-above-liquidus
outputs.desc: TAL for each TC location

outputs.name: process-window-index
outputs.desc: PWI score indicating how centered the profile is within the specification window

process: Run the first profile pass with the initial settings. Record the temperature-time data from all thermocouples. Plot the profiles overlaid with the specification window: ramp rate limits, soak temperature range, peak temperature range, time above liquidus range.

Calculate the process window index (PWI) for each TC location: PWI = max(abs((measured - center of spec) / (half width of spec))) across all specification parameters. A PWI of 0 means perfectly centered; PWI approaching 100% means at the specification edge. Target PWI < 70% for all TCs.

If the coldest TC peak temperature is below specification, increase the peak zone temperatures by 5C or decrease belt speed by 5%. If the hottest TC exceeds the maximum, decrease peak zone temperatures. Adjust one variable at a time and re-profile.

To reduce thermal delta: extend the soak zone (increase soak zone temperatures by 5-10C or decrease belt speed) to give the coldest region more time to absorb heat before the ramp to peak. Moving the soak setpoint closer to liquidus reduces the remaining temperature rise needed and thus reduces the delta at peak.

Iterate until all TCs simultaneously meet: peak temperature within specification, time above liquidus within specification, ramp rates within specification, and thermal delta within specification. Typically requires 3-5 profiling runs.
Record the final optimized profile as the production standard. Save the raw TC data files, the oven recipe (zone temperatures, belt speed, rail width), and the PWI calculation for each TC location.

steps.description: Evaluate nitrogen atmosphere, vacuum reflow, and vapor-phase reflow alternatives for improved joint quality, and determine cost-benefit for the specific product.

inputs.name: optimized-profile
inputs.desc: Baseline air reflow profile

inputs.name: thermal-delta-at-peak
inputs.desc: Thermal delta achieved in air reflow

inputs.name: component-thermal-ratings
inputs.desc: Temperature-sensitive components that constrain peak temperature

outputs.name: atmosphere-recommendation
outputs.desc: Air vs nitrogen vs vacuum vs vapor-phase recommendation with cost-benefit analysis

outputs.name: nitrogen-specification
outputs.desc: If nitrogen recommended: purity requirement (ppm O2), flow rate, and cost per board estimate

outputs.name: wetting-improvement-data
outputs.desc: Measured improvement in wetting angle and spread from reduced oxidation

outputs.name: voiding-reduction-data
outputs.desc: Void area reduction data for BGA and bottom-terminated components under the selected atmosphere

process: Nitrogen atmosphere reduces solder surface oxidation during reflow, improving wetting. The improvement is most significant for lead-free alloys which oxidize faster than SnPb. At <500ppm O2, wetting angle improves by 10-20 degrees for SAC305 on copper. At <100ppm O2, further improvement is marginal for most applications.

Evaluate whether nitrogen is justified for this product. The cost of nitrogen is $0.02-$0.10 per board depending on oven size and flow rate. The benefit is measurable for: fine-pitch components where marginal wetting causes opens, OSP board finish which degrades during reflow, and lead-free processes on thermally challenging boards where lower peak temperature is desired (nitrogen allows 5-10C lower peak).

For BGA voiding below 25% (IPC-7095 Class 3), nitrogen alone may be insufficient. Vacuum reflow (vacuum applied after peak temperature, during solidification) actively extracts entrapped flux volatiles, reducing void area to <5%. Cost is $0.50-$2.00 per board for vacuum-capable equipment.

Vapor-phase reflow (condensation soldering) provides inherent peak temperature control equal to the vapor temperature (230C for Galden LS230, 240C for LS240). This eliminates the risk of overheating and reduces thermal delta because the condensation rate self-limits on hotter surfaces. Cost is higher than convection reflow but may be justified for thermally sensitive assemblies.

Make the recommendation based on the specific product requirements. Standard commercial assembly: air reflow with proper profile optimization is usually sufficient. High-reliability or fine-pitch assembly: nitrogen reflow. Power electronics or high-current BGA: vacuum reflow for void reduction. Thermally sensitive mixed-technology: vapor-phase.

steps.description: Develop reflow strategies for boards with conflicting thermal requirements: mixed alloy, double-sided reflow, large thermal mass components alongside fine-pitch, and temperature-sensitive components.

inputs.name: optimized-profile
inputs.desc: Single-pass profile baseline

inputs.name: atmosphere-recommendation
inputs.desc: Atmosphere selection

inputs.name: board-assembly-drawing
inputs.desc: Full assembly showing both sides and all component types

inputs.name: component-thermal-ratings
inputs.desc: All component temperature limits

outputs.name: reflow-sequence
outputs.desc: Defined sequence for double-sided reflow including which side first and why

outputs.name: multi-pass-profile-set
outputs.desc: Profiles for each reflow pass with cumulative thermal exposure tracking

outputs.name: component-retention-strategy
outputs.desc: Strategy for preventing second-side component drop during the second reflow pass

outputs.name: mixed-technology-qualification-results
outputs.desc: Qualification data showing all joints meet specification after the full reflow sequence

process: For double-sided SMT, reflow the heavier side first (bottom side with larger components). During the second pass, the first side faces down and gravity acts on the components. Components stay in place if their weight does not exceed the surface tension of the molten solder. Rule of thumb: components under 0.1g stay; components over 0.5g need adhesive or mechanical retention.

Track cumulative thermal exposure. Each reflow pass subjects all previously soldered joints to another reflow cycle. Excessive reflow cycles cause intermetallic compound (IMC) growth: Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn. After 3+ reflow cycles, IMC thickness may exceed 5 microns, reducing joint ductility. For high-reliability products, limit total reflow passes to 2 plus 1 rework cycle.

For boards with mixed thermal mass (large power connector next to 0201 chips), consider local shielding. A reflective shield over temperature-sensitive components reduces their peak temperature by 5-15C during reflow without affecting the oven recipe. Alternatively, design the reflow profile with a longer soak to equalize temperatures before the peak.

For mixed-alloy assembly (leaded and lead-free components on the same board), the reflow temperature must be high enough to fully melt the lead-free alloy (217C for SAC305) which also melts SnPb (183C). The mixed alloy joint metallurgy is acceptable per IPC-J-STD-001 if wetting is adequate. However, backward compatibility testing should verify reliability.

Qualify the full reflow sequence as a system. Run the complete sequence (first side, flip, second side, any selective soldering) on profiler boards and verify all joints at all locations meet temperature and time specifications after the complete sequence. The first-side joints see the second reflow as an additional thermal cycle; verify they are still within IPC specifications.

description: Configure and optimize a wave soldering process for through-hole and mixed-technology boards, covering flux application, preheat, wave parameters, solder pot management, and defect elimination.

steps.description: Select and configure the flux application system for wave soldering, matching flux type to board requirements and setting application parameters for consistent coverage.

inputs.name: board-surface-finish

process: Select flux chemistry. For lead-free wave soldering, higher-activity flux is needed because SAC alloys wet more slowly than SnPb. Water-soluble ORL1 or ORH0 flux provides the best wetting for lead-free but requires aqueous cleaning within 4 hours of soldering. No-clean ROL0 or ROL1 flux is acceptable for SnPb and well-designed SAC processes but may leave visible residue.

Choose application method. Spray fluxing provides more uniform coverage and uses less flux than foam. Set spray nozzle air pressure, flux flow rate, and conveyor speed to achieve 500-1500 ug/cm2 of flux solids on the board bottom. Foam fluxing is simpler but wastes more flux and is less uniform at board edges.

Set specific gravity for the flux bath. The flux vendor provides the target specific gravity (typically 0.82-0.86 for spray fluxes). Monitor specific gravity daily with a hydrometer. Add thinner when SG rises (solvent evaporation concentrates the flux). Add flux concentrate when SG drops (contamination dilutes the flux).

Verify flux coverage using a test board with witness coupons. The solvent evaporates during preheat, leaving only the flux solids. Measure residue weight on a known area to confirm coverage. Alternatively, use a UV-fluorescent flux additive to visually inspect coverage uniformity.

steps.description: Configure wave solder preheat to activate flux, reduce thermal shock, and manage board temperature for reliable wetting, accounting for board mass and component sensitivity.

inputs.desc: Selected flux and its activation temperature range

inputs.name: board-surface-finish
inputs.desc: Board finish affecting preheat requirements

process: The preheat must accomplish three things simultaneously: activate the flux (typically requires 100-150C for 30-60 seconds), evaporate flux solvents to prevent spattering at the wave, and bring the board to a temperature that minimizes thermal shock when contacting the molten solder.

Set preheat to achieve a board topside temperature of 100-130C for tin-lead wave soldering and 110-145C for lead-free. The board bottom contacting the wave should be 10-20C higher than the topside. Insufficient preheat causes thermal shock (solder solidifies before filling barrels) and poor flux activation. Excessive preheat degrades flux activity and causes outgassing at the wave.

Configure preheat zones: bottom infrared heaters for direct board heating, top convection or IR for uniform heating of components. Ramp rate of 2-4C/s through the preheat zones. Total preheat time of 60-120 seconds depending on board thermal mass.

Verify flux activation by measuring the residue state after preheat. A properly activated flux will change from a wet, glossy appearance to a dry, matte appearance. Under-activated flux remains wet and will splatter at the wave. Over-activated flux is dry and charred, unable to clean oxides during soldering.

For lead-free wave soldering, higher preheat temperatures are critical because the solder pot is at 260-265C vs 245-250C for SnPb. The thermal gradient between board and solder must be managed to prevent barrel fill deficiency.

steps.description: Optimize wave soldering machine parameters including wave height, contact length, conveyor speed, and immersion depth for consistent barrel fill and minimal bridging.

inputs.name: board-topside-temperature
inputs.desc: Achieved board temperature from preheat

inputs.name: solder-alloy-type
inputs.desc: Alloy and pot temperature

inputs.name: component-types
inputs.desc: Through-hole component types (pin count, barrel diameter, lead finish)

outputs.desc: Length of solder contact from entry to exit, controlled by wave geometry and board angle

outputs.name: immersion-depth

process: Set wave height so the solder contacts the board bottom surface evenly across the full board width. The wave must be high enough to fill through-hole barrels by capillary action. For a dual-wave machine, set the chip wave (turbulent wave) height to contact the board for SMT components on the solder side, and the lambda wave (smooth wave) for through-hole barrel fill and bridge elimination.

Calculate contact time from conveyor speed and wave contact length. Contact time = contact length / conveyor speed. Target contact time of 2-4 seconds for SnPb and 3-5 seconds for lead-free (SAC alloys wet more slowly). For a 50mm wave contact length: 3 seconds requires a conveyor speed of 1 m/min.

Set immersion depth (also called penetration depth) to 50-75% of the board thickness. The solder should wick through the barrels by capillary action, not by pressure filling from the wave. Excessive immersion floods the board bottom and causes bridging. Insufficient immersion leaves barrels unfilled.

Adjust the board conveyor angle (typically 5-7 degrees from horizontal, trailing edge higher). This controls the peel-back of solder from the board as it exits the wave. A steeper angle improves drainage and reduces bridging but decreases contact time at the trailing edge.

For the chip wave (first wave, turbulent): set pump speed for aggressive flow to ensure solder contacts all surfaces of bottom-side SMT components in the wave shadow areas. For the lambda wave (second wave, smooth): set pump speed for a stable, laminar flow that does not disturb the chip wave solder and provides a clean peel-back.

steps.description: Monitor and manage solder pot chemistry to prevent contamination-related defects, including copper dissolution, gold embrittlement, and dross formation.

inputs.name: solder-alloy-type
inputs.desc: Base alloy composition

inputs.name: wave-contact-length
inputs.desc: Contact time and volume throughput affecting dissolution rate

inputs.name: board-surface-finish
inputs.desc: Board finish affecting contamination type (ENIG adds gold, OSP adds organics)

outputs.name: contamination-limits
outputs.desc: Maximum allowable levels for copper, gold, and other contaminants with analysis frequency

outputs.name: pot-maintenance-schedule
outputs.desc: Solder addition, dross removal, and pot cleaning schedule

outputs.name: contamination-monitoring-plan
outputs.desc: Sampling frequency and laboratory analysis requirements

outputs.name: pot-temperature-control
outputs.desc: Temperature setpoint and tolerance with calibration requirements

process: Copper dissolves from the board pads and component leads into the solder pot during wave contact. For SAC305, the copper saturation point is approximately 1.5% at 260C. Below saturation, copper dissolution from pads is aggressive (pad erosion). Above saturation, copper crystallizes out of solution and forms gritty joints. Monitor copper content and keep below 0.5% for SnPb and below 0.8% for SAC.

Gold from ENIG-finished boards dissolves rapidly into the pot. Gold content above 0.3% in SnPb causes gold embrittlement (AuSn4 intermetallic formation at grain boundaries makes joints brittle). For SAC, gold tolerance is slightly higher but should still be kept below 0.5%. Track gold content if processing ENIG boards regularly.

Dross (oxidized solder) forms on the pot surface continuously. Dross increases with pot temperature, wave turbulence, and air exposure. For SAC305, dross rate is higher than SnPb due to higher operating temperature. Remove dross before each production shift. Use nitrogen blanket over the pot surface to reduce dross formation by 50-80%.

Set pot temperature to alloy liquidus + 30-50C. For SnPb: 245-255C. For SAC305: 255-265C. Higher temperature improves wetting but increases copper dissolution rate, dross formation, and component thermal stress. Monitor pot temperature with an independent thermocouple (do not rely only on the machine thermocouple).

Sample the solder pot for chemical analysis monthly for low-volume production, weekly for high-volume. When contamination approaches limits, add fresh solder to dilute. When contamination exceeds limits, drain and replace the pot. Cost of a pot replacement is far less than the cost of contaminated solder defects.

steps.description: Identify and correct wave solder defects by mapping physical evidence to process parameters, with corrective actions for bridging, icicles, insufficient fill, blowholes, and solder balls.

inputs.name: conveyor-speed

process: Bridging (solder short between adjacent pins): caused by insufficient drainage at wave exit. Corrective actions: increase conveyor angle, decrease wave height, increase nitrogen flow at the peel-back zone, slow the conveyor to allow more drainage time. For fine-pitch connectors, ensure the lambda wave is smooth and laminar.

Icicles (pointed solder projections on pin tips): caused by solder wetting up the lead and solidifying during peel-back. Related to insufficient preheat (board too cold causes rapid solidification) or excessive wave contact (solder wets too high on the lead). Increase preheat temperature or reduce immersion depth.

Insufficient barrel fill (solder does not rise to the top side of the board): caused by insufficient preheat (capillary action fails because solder solidifies in the barrel), insufficient contact time, or poor flux activation. Verify board topside temperature exceeds 100C at the wave. Increase contact time or wave height. Check flux coverage.

Blowholes (voids in the solder fillet with a crater): caused by moisture or flux volatile outgassing during soldering. Moisture sources: absorbed moisture in the board laminate, component body, or flux. Increase preheat time and temperature to fully evaporate volatiles before wave contact. Bake moisture-sensitive boards per IPC-J-STD-033 before assembly.

Solder balls (small spheres on the board surface near wave-soldered joints): caused by solder spattering from flux outgassing at the wave, excessive dross on the pot surface, or turbulent wave contact. Ensure thorough preheat for flux activation, clean dross, and verify chip wave is not excessively turbulent.

Track defect rates by type using control charts. After each corrective action, run a statistically significant quantity (minimum 30 boards) and compare defect rates using a proportions test to verify the improvement is real, not random variation.

description: Predict and verify solder joint reliability using physics-of-failure models for thermal cycling, mechanical shock, and vibration, selecting alloy and pad design to meet the target service life.

steps.description: Identify the dominant fatigue mechanism for solder joints in the target application from the thermal and mechanical environment profile.

inputs.name: operating-environment
inputs.desc: Temperature range, number of thermal cycles per day/year, vibration spectrum, shock events expected over service life

inputs.name: component-package-types
inputs.desc: Package types on the board (BGA, QFP, chip resistors, connectors) with their CTE and standoff height

inputs.name: board-properties
inputs.desc: Board CTE, thickness, layer count, and mounting configuration

inputs.name: target-service-life
inputs.desc: Required service life in years and failure rate target

outputs.name: dominant-failure-mechanism
outputs.desc: Primary failure mechanism (thermal fatigue, vibration fatigue, mechanical shock, or combination) with ranking

outputs.name: critical-joints
outputs.desc: Component locations most susceptible to fatigue failure, ranked by stress level

outputs.name: cte-mismatch-analysis
outputs.desc: CTE mismatch between each component package and the board, driving shear strain in solder joints

outputs.name: fatigue-life-drivers
outputs.desc: The parameters that most affect joint life for this application (temperature range, dwell time, vibration frequency, DNP)

process: Calculate the CTE mismatch for each component type. Board CTE is typically 14-18 ppm/C for FR-4 (depends on copper content and resin system). Ceramic packages (CBGA, ceramic chip capacitors) have CTE of 6-7 ppm/C. Plastic packages (PBGA, QFP) have CTE of 15-25 ppm/C depending on mold compound. The mismatch drives shear strain in the solder joint during thermal excursions.

Identify the distance from neutral point (DNP) for area array packages (BGA). The outermost solder balls experience the highest shear strain: strain = (CTE_mismatch x delta_T x DNP) / solder_joint_height. A 35mm BGA with 0.5mm standoff, 10 ppm/C mismatch, and 100C cycle range produces approximately 2% shear strain at the corner balls.

For thermal fatigue, shear strain is the primary driver. For vibration fatigue, bending stress from board flexure dominates, and the joints nearest the board edges or mounting points see the highest stress. For mechanical shock (drop), the strain rate is high, and the failure mode shifts from bulk solder fatigue to pad cratering (fracture in the board laminate under the pad).

Rank the failure mechanisms by the product application. Automotive underhood: thermal cycling dominates (−40 to +125C, 10+ years, 1000+ cycles). Consumer handheld: mechanical shock (drop) and vibration dominate. Telecom infrastructure: thermal cycling at narrow range (20 to 55C) over 20 years, vibration from fans.

Identify the critical joints: corner balls of the largest BGA (highest DNP), small chip components in high-flex zones (vibration), and components near board edges (shock). These locations should receive design attention and will be the focus of reliability testing.

steps.description: Apply the Coffin-Manson strain-life model and Norris-Landzberg acceleration factor to predict solder joint thermal fatigue life from accelerated test data.

inputs.name: cte-mismatch-analysis
inputs.desc: CTE mismatch and DNP data for critical components

inputs.name: dominant-failure-mechanism
inputs.desc: Confirmation that thermal fatigue is the primary mechanism

inputs.name: operating-environment
inputs.desc: Field temperature cycling profile

inputs.name: target-service-life
inputs.desc: Required cycles to failure at the target failure probability

outputs.name: predicted-field-life
outputs.desc: Predicted number of thermal cycles to failure in the field for each critical joint

outputs.name: acceleration-factor
outputs.desc: Ratio of field cycles to test cycles for the selected test profile

outputs.name: test-duration
outputs.desc: Number of accelerated test cycles needed to demonstrate the target field life

outputs.name: alloy-comparison
outputs.desc: Predicted life comparison for SAC305 vs SAC105 vs SnPb under the field conditions

process: Calculate shear strain range for each critical joint: gamma = (alpha_substrate - alpha_component) x delta_T x L / h, where alpha is CTE, delta_T is temperature range, L is distance from neutral point, and h is joint height (standoff). This is the strain imposed on the solder each thermal cycle.

Apply the Coffin-Manson equation: Nf = C x (gamma)^(-n), where Nf is cycles to failure, gamma is the plastic strain range, and C and n are material constants. For SAC305: n is approximately 1.9-2.2, C depends on the specific joint geometry and test method. For SnPb: n is approximately 1.8-2.0. These constants are derived from cyclic shear testing of actual solder joints, not bulk material data.

To predict field life from accelerated test data, apply the Norris-Landzberg acceleration factor: AF = (delta_T_test / delta_T_field)^m x (f_field / f_test)^n x exp(Ea/k x (1/T_max_field - 1/T_max_test)), where m is approximately 2.0 for SAC, n is approximately 0.33, Ea is 0.122 eV (activation energy for SAC grain boundary sliding). This accounts for temperature range, cycling frequency, and maximum temperature effects.

Design the accelerated test to achieve the target field life in a reasonable test duration. For automotive (1000+ field cycles over 10 years), a test profile of -40 to +125C with 30-minute dwell provides an acceleration factor of approximately 3-5x over the mild field cycle. The test duration is: test cycles = field cycles / AF.

Compare alloys. SAC305 generally outperforms SnPb in thermal cycling at wide temperature ranges (automotive) but may underperform at narrow ranges with high dwell times (telecom). SAC105 has lower thermal fatigue resistance than SAC305 but better drop shock performance. Select the alloy that is best for the dominant failure mechanism.

Apply the Weibull distribution to test results. Thermal fatigue failures follow a Weibull distribution with shape parameter (beta) typically 3-6 for solder joints. Use maximum likelihood estimation to fit the Weibull parameters from accelerated test data and extrapolate to the target failure probability (e.g., 1% failure at 10 years).

steps.description: Optimize pad geometry, via configuration, and solder mask design to maximize solder joint reliability for the critical components identified in the fatigue analysis.

inputs.name: predicted-field-life

inputs.name: component-package-types

outputs.desc: Optimized pad geometry for each critical component type with rationale

outputs.desc: SMD vs NSMD (copper-defined) pad selection for BGA with reliability implications

outputs.name: via-in-pad-specification
outputs.desc: Via-in-pad requirements for thermal or routing purposes with reliability impact

outputs.name: reliability-improvement-estimate
outputs.desc: Estimated life improvement from pad design changes

process: For BGA pads, choose between solder-mask-defined (SMD) and non-solder-mask-defined (NSMD/copper-defined) pads. NSMD pads allow the solder to wet the copper pad edge, creating a larger interface area and typically 20-30% better thermal fatigue life. However, SMD pads provide a larger copper area that resists pad cratering under mechanical shock. For automotive thermal cycling: NSMD. For consumer drop shock: SMD.

Optimize BGA pad diameter. The pad diameter affects the solder joint height (standoff) and volume. Larger pads reduce standoff (solder ball spreads more), increasing shear strain per cycle. Pad diameter of 80-100% of the ball diameter is typical. For maximum thermal fatigue life, target the largest standoff that still provides reliable alignment and self-centering during reflow.

For chip components (0201, 0402, 0603), pad length extension beyond the component end controls fillet size. Longer pads create larger fillets with lower peak stress at the fillet toe. IPC-7351 provides pad geometry recommendations by component size. For vibration-critical applications, extend pads 0.2-0.4mm beyond the component end.

Via-in-pad for BGA: if vias must be in the pad for routing, they must be filled and planarized (plugged with epoxy and copper-capped). Unfilled vias under BGA pads cause paste migration into the via during reflow, resulting in voids and reduced joint volume. Filled and capped vias add manufacturing cost but eliminate this failure mode.

For solder-mask opening on QFP/QFN pads, specify 1:1 or slight mask expansion (50-75um per side). Excessive mask opening allows solder to flow onto adjacent traces. Insufficient opening reduces the wetting area. For QFN (bottom-terminated), the thermal pad mask opening pattern controls voiding: a segmented opening (cross or window pattern) allows flux volatiles to escape.

steps.description: Execute solder joint reliability testing per the life prediction model, including thermal cycling, drop shock, and vibration, with failure analysis at each readout interval.

inputs.desc: Calculated acceleration factor for the test profile

inputs.name: test-duration
inputs.desc: Required number of test cycles

inputs.name: pad-design-recommendations
inputs.desc: Optimized pad designs to validate

process: Prepare test vehicles. For thermal cycling: daisy-chain test boards with resistance monitoring on each critical component. Continuity monitor logs resistance continuously during cycling. A resistance increase above 20% from baseline indicates crack initiation. A resistance increase to infinity (open circuit) indicates complete failure.

For thermal cycling: use IEC 60749-25 or JEDEC JESD22-A104. Set the chamber to the specified temperature range with transition time of 10-15 minutes between extremes and dwell time of 10-15 minutes at each extreme. Monitor all daisy chains continuously. Readout intervals at 250, 500, 1000, 1500, and 2000 cycles (or until target cycles are reached).

For drop shock testing: use JEDEC JESD22-B111 (board-level drop). Mount the test board on a drop table with specified weight and standoff. Drop conditions: 1500G peak, 0.5ms half-sine pulse. Monitor all daisy chains for intermittent opens. Continue drops until the specified number of drops (typically 30-100) or until failure criterion is met (3 consecutive events at any component).

At each readout interval, remove samples for cross-section analysis. Cross-section through the critical solder joints. Measure crack length as a fraction of the joint width. Identify crack location (bulk solder, intermetallic interface, pad interface) to determine the failure mode. Photograph the crack under SEM to characterize the fracture surface (intergranular fatigue, transgranular, intermetallic fracture).

Fit the failure data to a Weibull distribution using maximum likelihood estimation. Plot on Weibull probability paper. Extract the shape parameter (beta, indicating failure mode consistency) and characteristic life (eta, cycles at 63.2% failure). Apply the Norris-Landzberg acceleration factor to convert test life to field life. Compare to the target service life requirement.

Document the qualification results as a formal test report. Include the test conditions, sample sizes, failure distributions, failure analysis, and the field life prediction with confidence intervals. If the predicted field life meets or exceeds the target, the design is qualified.

description: Design and optimize an automated inspection strategy using AOI, SPI, and X-ray to maximize defect detection while minimizing false calls, with programming methodology and correlation analysis.

steps.description: Define the inspection points, equipment allocation, and coverage targets for the SMT line based on product risk and defect escape cost.

inputs.name: product-risk-level
inputs.desc: Consequence of a defect escape to the end customer (safety-critical, high-reliability, commercial)

inputs.name: board-complexity
inputs.desc: Component count, BGA/QFN presence, finest pitch, double-sided assembly

inputs.name: production-volume
inputs.desc: Annual volume affecting the economics of inspection equipment investment

inputs.name: historical-defect-data
inputs.desc: Known defect types and rates from similar products or prototype builds

outputs.name: inspection-point-map
outputs.desc: Where in the process each inspection occurs (post-print SPI, post-placement pre-reflow, post-reflow AOI, X-ray) with coverage scope at each point

outputs.name: coverage-target
outputs.desc: Target defect coverage percentage for each defect type at each inspection point

outputs.name: equipment-requirements
outputs.desc: AOI, SPI, and X-ray equipment specifications needed to achieve the coverage targets

outputs.name: sampling-vs-100pct

process: Map each defect type to the earliest inspection point where it can be detected. Paste defects (insufficient, excess, bridging, offset) are detected at SPI. Placement defects (missing, shifted, wrong part, polarity) are detected at post-placement AOI. Solder defects (bridging, insufficient, tombstone, cold joint) are detected at post-reflow AOI. Hidden joint defects (BGA voids, head-in-pillow, QFN voiding) are detected only by X-ray.

For safety-critical and high-reliability products: 100% SPI + 100% post-reflow AOI + 100% X-ray for all BGA/QFN/hidden joints. For commercial products: 100% SPI + 100% post-reflow AOI + X-ray sampling (sample size based on AQL). For high-volume consumer: SPI on every board, AOI on every board, X-ray only on first articles and triggered by SPC out-of-control events.

Calculate the cost of a defect escape at each stage. Catching a paste defect at SPI costs pennies (rework before components are placed). Catching it at post-reflow AOI costs dollars (rework a soldered board). Missing it entirely costs hundreds to thousands (field return, warranty, safety recall). This cost ratio justifies early detection investment.

Define the false call target. A false call rate above 500ppm (0.05%) causes operator fatigue and leads to real defects being dismissed. Target <200ppm false calls for post-reflow AOI and <100ppm for SPI. Achieving low false call rates requires careful program optimization, not just accepting machine defaults.

steps.description: Develop the AOI inspection program with component library setup, algorithm selection, and threshold optimization to achieve the target detection rate with minimum false calls.

inputs.desc: Inspection points and coverage scope

outputs.name: false-call-rate

outputs.name: defect-detection-rate

process: Build the component library entry for each unique component. Teach the machine the expected appearance: body outline, terminal locations, polarity marks, marking text. Use golden board images (known-good boards) as the reference. Teach from multiple boards to capture normal variation in component appearance, solder joint finish, and board color.

Select inspection algorithms per component type. For chip components (0201-0805): solder fillet presence, height, and wetting angle. For QFP/SOP: bridging detection between adjacent leads, solder volume on each lead. For BGA: check for missing balls using X-ray or peripheral ball inspection via AOI (AOI cannot inspect center balls). For passives: polarity mark verification. For connectors: pin coplanarity and solder fill.

Set initial thresholds conservatively (tight limits) and run 30+ boards through the AOI. Collect all defect calls and manually classify each as real defect or false call. For each false call, determine the cause: threshold too tight, reference image variation, lighting artifact, or component variation.

Loosen thresholds only for the specific algorithm generating false calls, not globally. Use multiple inspection windows per component: one for solder presence (tight threshold), another for cosmetic variation (looser threshold). This maintains high detection for real defects while tolerating normal cosmetic variation.

Validate the detection rate using a test board with known defects. Either create defect coupons (intentionally misplaced components, bridged pads, insufficient solder applied with syringe) or collect real defect samples during optimization. Verify that the AOI detects all planted defects. Repeat for each defect type.

Measure the final false call rate over 100+ production boards. Target < 200ppm (fewer than 1 false call per 5000 component inspections). Document the verification results and lock the program for production.

steps.description: Correlate SPI measurements to post-reflow defect outcomes to set predictive SPI limits that prevent defects rather than just detecting paste anomalies.

inputs.name: aoi-program
inputs.desc: Post-reflow AOI detection capability

inputs.name: inspection-point-map
inputs.desc: SPI and AOI inspection coverage

inputs.name: historical-defect-data
inputs.desc: Past defect data for correlation

outputs.name: spi-defect-correlation
outputs.desc: Statistical correlation between SPI metrics (volume, height, area, offset) and post-reflow defect types

outputs.name: predictive-spi-limits
outputs.desc: SPI alarm limits derived from correlation that predict defects rather than using arbitrary percentage limits

outputs.name: spi-rejection-criteria
outputs.desc: Board-level and pad-level SPI criteria for rejection before placement to prevent known defect outcomes

process: Collect paired data: SPI measurements (volume, height, area, offset for every pad) and post-reflow AOI results (defect/no-defect for every joint) for a minimum of 500 boards. This requires data export from both systems and matching by board serial number and pad location.

For each defect type, analyze the SPI distribution of defective vs non-defective joints. Bridging correlates with paste volume (excess) and paste offset. Insufficient solder correlates with paste volume (low) and paste area (small). Tombstoning correlates with paste volume asymmetry between the two pads of a chip component.

Set SPI limits based on the correlation data rather than using the default +/-50% volume limits. For example, if bridging on 0.5mm pitch QFP occurs when paste volume exceeds 140% of nominal but never below 130%, set the SPI upper alarm at 130% (with margin). If insufficient solder occurs below 60% volume, set the lower alarm at 65%.

Implement pad-level and board-level SPI rejection criteria. Pad-level: reject the board at the SPI stage if any pad exceeds the defect-correlated limit for a critical defect type. Board-level: reject if more than N pads are out of the process control limits (even if none individually exceed the defect limit). The board-level criterion catches systematic process drift.

Re-validate the correlation quarterly or when the process changes (new paste batch, new stencil, new board revision). Paste rheology variation and stencil wear change the SPI-to-defect relationship over time.
