outputs.desc: Inspection time per board and impact on line throughput, with sampling strategy if 100% is not feasible

process: For BGA solder joint inspection, capture a 2D top-down view. Each solder ball should appear as a consistent-density circle. Missing balls appear as absent circles. Bridges appear as connected adjacent circles. Voids appear as lighter areas within the ball image (less solder density). Head-in-pillow appears as a double-density ring (two spheres not coalescenced).

Measure void area using image processing. The void area ratio = total void area / total pad area x 100%. Per IPC-7095: Class 3 maximum is 25% void area per individual joint, with an additional package-level limit of 25% average void area. Class 2 is 30%. For power components where thermal performance depends on solder joint thermal resistance, specify <10% or <5% voiding.

For head-in-pillow detection, the 2D top-down view may show a double ring pattern (paste hemisphere and ball hemisphere side by side rather than merged). Oblique angle inspection (tilting the board 30-45 degrees to the X-ray beam) more clearly reveals HiP defects as the separation between the two hemispheres becomes visible as a shadow.

For QFN thermal pad inspection, capture a view centered on the thermal pad. Void distribution matters as much as total void area. One large central void is worse than multiple small distributed voids for thermal performance. Specify both total void area (<25%) and maximum single void size (<10% of pad area) for QFN thermal pads.

Assess X-ray throughput impact. 2D inspection of one BGA takes 5-15 seconds depending on automation level. A board with 4 BGAs takes 30-60 seconds for X-ray vs 5-10 seconds for AOI. For high-volume lines, 100% X-ray may limit throughput. Use statistical sampling (e.g., AQL level I or II) for production with 100% inspection reserved for first articles, lot starts, and SPC triggers.

description: Analyze and improve manufacturing yield using statistical methods from first-pass yield calculation through defect Pareto, root cause analysis, SPC, and yield learning curves for new product introduction.

steps.description: Calculate yield metrics from production data: first-pass yield, rolled throughput yield, DPMO, and sigma level, establishing the baseline for improvement.

inputs.name: production-data
inputs.desc: Board count, defect count by type, rework count, scrap count for the analysis period

inputs.name: component-count-per-board
inputs.desc: Total component count and opportunity count per defect type

inputs.name: test-coverage-data
inputs.desc: Defect detection rates at each inspection and test stage

outputs.name: first-pass-yield
outputs.desc: Percentage of boards passing all tests and inspections without rework on the first attempt

outputs.name: rolled-throughput-yield
outputs.desc: Probability of a board passing through all process stages without requiring rework at any stage

outputs.name: dpmo-and-sigma
outputs.desc: Defects per million opportunities and equivalent sigma level for the assembly process

outputs.name: hidden-factory-cost
outputs.desc: Cost of rework and scrap as a percentage of production cost, representing the hidden factory

process: Calculate first-pass yield (FPY): FPY = (boards passing first time) / (total boards started) x 100%. This is the simplest yield metric but hides rework. A line with 92% FPY and 7% rework appears to ship 99% but consumes significant hidden factory effort.

Calculate rolled throughput yield (RTY): RTY = Y_print x Y_placement x Y_reflow x Y_AOI x Y_test, where each Y is the first-pass yield at that stage. RTY is always lower than final yield because it compounds rework probability. A process with 98% yield at each of 5 stages has RTY = 0.98^5 = 90.4%, meaning only 90.4% of boards pass through without any rework.

Calculate DPMO: DPMO = (total defects / total opportunities) x 1,000,000. Define opportunities carefully: for a 500-component board, the minimum opportunity count is 500 (one per component). A more granular count counts each solder joint as an opportunity (a 500-component board with average 3 joints per component = 1500 opportunities). Use the same opportunity definition consistently for trending.

Convert DPMO to sigma level using the standard normal distribution. 3.4 DPMO = 6 sigma. 233 DPMO = 5 sigma. 6,210 DPMO = 4 sigma. 66,807 DPMO = 3 sigma. A typical SMT line operates at 4.0-4.5 sigma. World-class SMT is 5.0 sigma or better.

Calculate the hidden factory cost: sum of all rework labor, rework materials, scrap, and inspection operator time spent verifying false calls and diagnosing defects. This cost is often 5-15% of the direct production cost and is the target for yield improvement projects.

steps.description: Construct a defect Pareto from inspection and test data, then apply structured root cause analysis to the top defect contributors to identify corrective actions.

inputs.name: first-pass-yield
inputs.desc: Current yield baseline

inputs.name: dpmo-and-sigma
inputs.desc: Current quality level

inputs.name: production-data
inputs.desc: Detailed defect data by type, location, and time

inputs.name: hidden-factory-cost
inputs.desc: Cost of each defect type for prioritization

outputs.name: defect-pareto
outputs.desc: Ranked list of defect types by frequency and cost, showing cumulative percentage

outputs.name: root-cause-analysis
outputs.desc: 5-why and fishbone analysis results for the top 3 defect types

outputs.name: corrective-action-plan
outputs.desc: Specific process changes to address each root cause with expected yield improvement

outputs.name: verification-plan
outputs.desc: How to measure whether each corrective action was effective

process: Build the defect Pareto chart. Rank defect types by frequency. Typically, 3-5 defect types account for 80% of all defects (Pareto principle). The top defect type is the first improvement target unless a lower-frequency defect has disproportionately high cost (e.g., a rare defect that causes field failure vs. a common cosmetic defect caught at AOI).

For each of the top 3 defect types, apply the 5-why method. Start with the defect observation and ask why it occurred. Each answer becomes the subject of the next why. Continue until you reach a root cause that is actionable (a process parameter, material property, or design characteristic that can be changed). Typically requires 3-5 levels of why.

Supplement the 5-why with a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram organizing potential causes by the 6M categories: Machine (equipment settings, maintenance), Method (process procedure, recipe), Material (solder paste, components, board), Man (operator technique, training), Measurement (inspection criteria, calibration), and Environment (temperature, humidity, ESD). This ensures you do not miss contributing factors.

For each root cause, define a corrective action with a responsible person and target completion date. The corrective action must be specific and measurable. Not 'improve the print process' but 'reduce squeegee speed from 80mm/s to 60mm/s to increase paste volume transfer efficiency on 0201 pads from 72% to 85%.'

Define the verification method for each corrective action. Run a statistically significant quantity of boards after the change (minimum 30 boards, preferably 100+) and compare the defect rate to the baseline using a proportions test (chi-square or Fisher's exact). A p-value < 0.05 confirms the improvement is statistically significant, not random variation.

steps.description: Select and configure the appropriate statistical process control charts for each critical-to-quality parameter, with control limits calculated from process data rather than specification limits.

inputs.name: defect-pareto
inputs.desc: Top defect types driving the need for SPC

inputs.name: corrective-action-plan
inputs.desc: Process parameters to monitor after corrective actions

inputs.name: production-data
inputs.desc: Historical process data for control limit calculation

outputs.name: spc-chart-assignments
outputs.desc: Chart type and parameters for each monitored characteristic

outputs.name: control-limits
outputs.desc: Calculated UCL, CL, LCL for each chart from process data

outputs.name: out-of-control-rules
outputs.desc: Western Electric rules applied and the response procedure for each alarm type

outputs.name: process-capability-baseline
outputs.desc: Cpk and Ppk values for each monitored parameter

process: Select chart type by data type. For continuous measurements (paste volume, placement offset, reflow peak temperature): X-bar and R chart for subgroup data, Individuals and Moving Range (I-MR) chart for single measurements. For attribute data (defect counts): p-chart for fraction defective (constant or variable sample size), u-chart for defects per unit (when multiple defects per board are possible), c-chart for count of defects (constant sample size).

Calculate control limits from process data, never from specification limits. Collect 25 or more subgroups of data while the process is in control (no known assignable causes). Calculate the mean and control limits using standard formulas: UCL = X-bar + A2*R-bar, LCL = X-bar - A2*R-bar for X-bar charts. Control limits represent the voice of the process; specification limits represent the voice of the customer. They are different things.

Calculate process capability. Cp = (USL - LSL) / (6 x sigma), where sigma is estimated from R-bar/d2. Cpk = min((USL - X-bar) / (3*sigma), (X-bar - LSL) / (3*sigma)). Target Cpk > 1.33 for general processes, Cpk > 1.67 for safety-critical. If Cpk < 1.0, the process is not capable and will produce defects even when in statistical control.

Apply Western Electric rules for out-of-control detection: Rule 1 (one point beyond 3-sigma), Rule 2 (9 points in a row on the same side of the center line), Rule 3 (6 points in a row steadily increasing or decreasing), Rule 4 (14 points in a row alternating up and down). Each rule detects a different type of process shift.

Define the reaction plan for each alarm type. Rule 1 violation: stop production, investigate the assignable cause, correct and verify before restarting. Rule 2 violation (shift): investigate gradual drift (tool wear, material lot change). Rule 3 violation (trend): investigate progressive change (paste aging, temperature drift). Document the reaction plan as part of the control plan.

steps.description: Model and accelerate the yield learning curve during new product introduction, setting realistic yield targets and ramp milestones from prototype through volume production.

inputs.name: process-capability-baseline
inputs.desc: Current process capability for each parameter

inputs.name: first-pass-yield
inputs.desc: Current baseline yield

inputs.name: board-complexity
inputs.desc: Component count and mix for the new product

inputs.name: historical-defect-data
inputs.desc: Yield ramp data from similar past product introductions

outputs.name: yield-ramp-model
outputs.desc: Predicted yield trajectory from first build through steady-state production with milestones

outputs.name: yield-targets-by-build
outputs.desc: Yield target for each production build phase (proto, pilot, ramp, steady-state)

outputs.name: acceleration-actions
outputs.desc: Specific actions to accelerate the learning curve (pre-production DFM fixes, test vehicle builds, process tuning)

outputs.name: steady-state-yield-prediction
outputs.desc: Predicted mature yield based on process capability and board complexity

process: Estimate steady-state yield from process capability and component count. If the process DPMO is 50 (approximately 4.8 sigma) and the board has 1500 solder joint opportunities, expected defect rate per board = 1500 x 50/1,000,000 = 0.075 defects/board. FPY = e^(-0.075) = 92.8% (Poisson approximation). This is the theoretical steady-state yield if no new defect modes are introduced.

Model the yield learning curve. Wright's learning curve model: Y(n) = Y_mature x (1 - b x e^(-n/tau)), where n is cumulative boards built, b is the initial yield gap (typically 0.15-0.30 for SMT), and tau is the learning rate constant (depends on process maturity and improvement effort). A typical SMT yield ramp reaches 80% of mature yield by 500 boards and 95% by 2000 boards.

Set yield targets by build phase. Prototype (first 10-50 boards): target 70-80% of mature yield, focus on defect discovery and design corrections. Pilot (50-500 boards): target 85-90% of mature yield, focus on process optimization and SPC setup. Ramp (500-5000 boards): target 95% of mature yield, focus on fine-tuning and sustained improvement. Steady-state (5000+): target 100% of mature yield with continuous improvement beyond.

Identify acceleration actions. Pre-production DFM review catches design-related yield losses before the first build. Process tuning using SPI and AOI data from the prototype build corrects parameter settings early. Test vehicle builds (unpopulated or partially populated boards run through the line) tune the process without consuming production material.

Track actual yield against the learning curve model after each build. If actual yield lags the model, investigate: are new defect modes appearing that were not in the model? Is the process drifting? Are incoming materials (paste, components, boards) varying? Update the model with actual data to improve prediction accuracy for future NPI programs.

description: Execute a manufacturing new product introduction from DFM review through prototype builds, process qualification, and production release, with quality gates at each phase.

steps.description: Review the PCB design against specific manufacturing process capabilities, flagging features that exceed process limits or reduce yield, with quantified risk for each item.

inputs.name: pcb-design-data
inputs.desc: Gerber files, BOM, assembly drawings, and pick-and-place centroid data

inputs.name: process-capability-data
inputs.desc: Documented capabilities of the target assembly line (finest pitch, smallest component, minimum annular ring, etc.)

inputs.name: ipc-class-requirement
inputs.desc: Target IPC-610 class level (1, 2, or 3) for the product

outputs.name: dfm-issues-list
outputs.desc: Each DFM issue with severity (critical/major/minor), affected components, and recommended design change

outputs.name: yield-risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Estimated yield impact of each DFM issue if not addressed

outputs.name: design-change-requests
outputs.desc: Formal requests to the design team for DFM corrections before prototype build

outputs.name: process-deviation-list
outputs.desc: Issues that will require non-standard process parameters if the design is not changed

process: Check component pitch against stencil printing capability. If the process is qualified for 0.5mm pitch QFP but the design uses 0.4mm pitch, this requires a thinner stencil or step-down stencil and finer paste. Quantify: expected yield loss for 0.4mm pitch with existing 0.1mm stencil vs. required 0.08mm stencil.

Check component-to-component spacing against placement machine accuracy and rework access. Minimum spacing for machine placement is typically 0.3mm between bodies. For rework, minimum 1.5mm between tall components. Flag any spacing violations with the specific component reference designators.

Check pad design against IPC-7351 and the process capability. Verify annular ring meets IPC class requirement (Class 2: 0.05mm min, Class 3: 0.05mm min external, 0.025mm internal). Check via-in-pad requirements for BGA fanout. Verify thermal relief connections on large pads to prevent wicking.

Check for tombstoning risk on small passive components. Asymmetric copper connections to a pad pair (one pad connected to a ground plane, the other to a narrow trace) cause unequal reflow heating and tombstoning. Recommend thermal relief on the ground-connected pad or increasing trace width to the other pad.

Check testability. Are test points accessible for ICT/flying probe? Is the board panelized with breakaway tabs that do not damage components? Are fiducials present for machine alignment (minimum 3, not obscured by components)? Flag each missing testability feature.

Compile the DFM report sorted by severity. Critical issues (will cause defects or are unmanufacturable) must be resolved before prototype build. Major issues (will reduce yield or increase cost) should be resolved before pilot production. Minor issues (cosmetic or best-practice) are tracked for the next design revision.

steps.description: Plan and execute the prototype build with process documentation, deviation tracking, and structured defect collection to feed back into design and process improvements.

inputs.name: dfm-issues-list
inputs.desc: Known DFM issues and their resolution status

inputs.name: process-deviation-list
inputs.desc: Required process deviations for this build

inputs.name: pcb-design-data
inputs.desc: Latest design revision

inputs.name: ipc-class-requirement
inputs.desc: Quality class for workmanship acceptance

outputs.name: build-report
outputs.desc: Detailed report of the prototype build: quantities, yields, defect log, and process observations

outputs.name: design-feedback
outputs.desc: Design issues discovered during assembly that were not caught in DFM review

outputs.name: process-parameter-baseline
outputs.desc: Documented process parameters used for the prototype build as the starting point for optimization

outputs.name: bill-of-process
outputs.desc: Assembly sequence, tooling requirements, and special handling instructions documented from the prototype experience

process: Before the build, prepare a build traveler documenting: board revision, BOM revision, quantity, required process deviations from standard, inspection requirements, and test requirements. Each deviation must have an engineering justification and an owner responsible for resolving it before pilot production.

During the build, log every defect with: type, location (reference designator), root cause (if known), and corrective action taken (rework method, scrap). Use a structured defect log, not informal notes. This data feeds the yield prediction model.

Capture process parameters for each stage. Print: paste type, stencil ID, printer settings. Placement: program revision, feeder assignments, nozzle assignments. Reflow: profile data file, oven recipe. These parameters become the starting point for process optimization. Any changes made during the build are documented as deviations.

After the build, perform a structured build review. Compare actual yield to prediction. Classify each defect as design-related (DFM issue), process-related (parameter optimization needed), material-related (component or board quality), or operator-related (training gap). Each classification drives a different corrective action path.

Issue design change requests for any design-related defects discovered during the build. These must be resolved before the pilot build. Track resolution of each DCR and verify the fix in the next build revision.

steps.description: Qualify the assembly process for volume production through process capability studies, equipment qualification, and documentation of the standard operating procedures.

inputs.name: process-parameter-baseline
inputs.desc: Parameters from prototype build

inputs.name: build-report
inputs.desc: Prototype build results for baseline

inputs.name: bill-of-process
inputs.desc: Assembly sequence and tooling list

inputs.name: ipc-class-requirement
inputs.desc: Quality class for qualification criteria

outputs.name: process-qualification-report
outputs.desc: Capability studies for each critical process parameter demonstrating Cpk > 1.33 (or 1.67 for Class 3)

outputs.name: standard-operating-procedures
outputs.desc: Documented SOPs for each assembly process stage with parameter settings and operator instructions

outputs.name: control-plan
outputs.desc: Control plan linking process parameters to inspection methods, control limits, and reaction plans

outputs.name: production-readiness-assessment
outputs.desc: Checklist of qualification criteria met and any open items for production release

process: Run a process capability study on the pilot build (minimum 30 boards, preferably 100). Measure critical parameters: SPI paste volume on critical pads, placement accuracy on finest pitch components, reflow peak temperature and TAL on profiled boards. Calculate Cpk for each parameter. All critical parameters must demonstrate Cpk > 1.33 for Class 2, Cpk > 1.67 for Class 3.

Qualify the equipment: verify that each machine (printer, pick-and-place, oven, AOI, test) meets its specification under production conditions. This is not a machine acceptance test (which happens at installation) but a confirmation that the machine produces conforming output with the specific product at production speed.

Write standard operating procedures for each process stage. Each SOP contains: purpose, equipment settings (exact parameters), material requirements, operator steps, inspection criteria, and reaction to out-of-spec conditions. SOPs are the production floor reference; they must be specific enough that a trained operator can set up and run the process without engineering support.

Build the control plan. For each process step, the control plan specifies: what is controlled (parameter), how it is measured (method and equipment), how often (frequency), what are the limits (control and specification), and what to do when limits are exceeded (reaction plan). The control plan is the bridge between the process qualification data and the ongoing production monitoring.

Conduct the production readiness assessment. Checklist includes: all DFM issues resolved or accepted with risk documentation, process capability demonstrated, SOPs released, control plan in place, SPC charts set up, operators trained and certified, materials qualified and in stock, test equipment correlated to design verification results. Any open item is a condition for limited production release.

steps.description: Make the formal production release decision based on qualification data, yield trajectory, and risk assessment, with conditions for limited vs full release.

inputs.name: process-qualification-report
inputs.desc: All capability study results

inputs.name: production-readiness-assessment
inputs.desc: Qualification checklist status

inputs.name: control-plan
inputs.desc: Monitoring plan for ongoing production

inputs.name: standard-operating-procedures
inputs.desc: SOP release status

outputs.name: production-release-authorization
outputs.desc: Formal go/no-go/conditional decision with signatures and conditions

outputs.name: open-item-tracker
outputs.desc: Any open items from qualification with owners, due dates, and interim risk mitigations

outputs.name: lessons-learned-log
outputs.desc: Process and design lessons from the NPI that apply to future products

outputs.name: npi-closure-report
outputs.desc: Summary of the NPI project: timeline, yield progression, cost, and recommendations for future NPI improvements

process: Review all qualification evidence. If all criteria are met (Cpk targets, yield targets, documentation complete, training complete), issue a full production release. If most criteria are met with minor open items, issue a conditional release with specific limitations (e.g., increased inspection frequency, limited lot size, engineering monitoring of the first N production lots).

For a conditional release, define the conditions clearly: what must be resolved, by when, and what happens if the conditions are not met by the deadline. Assign an owner for each condition. Track conditions in the open item tracker. Escalate if conditions are not resolved on schedule.

Capture lessons learned while they are fresh. Categorize by: design lessons (DFM issues that should be added to the design checklist), process lessons (parameter windows that were tighter than expected), material lessons (component or board quality issues), and project management lessons (timeline, resource, or communication issues).

Issue the NPI closure report. This document summarizes the entire NPI from initial DFM review through production release: timeline vs plan, yield progression vs model, total NPI cost, and recommendations. This becomes the reference for future NPI programs of similar complexity.

Hand off to production. Transfer ownership of the control plan, SOPs, and open items from the NPI engineering team to the production engineering team. The first 3-5 production lots should have engineering review of all quality data to verify that the transition is smooth and no new issues emerge.

description: Select, apply, and verify conformal coating on electronic assemblies for environmental protection, covering coating type selection, masking, application, cure, inspection, and rework.

steps.description: Select the conformal coating chemistry from application requirements: operating environment, temperature range, rework needs, and regulatory compliance.

inputs.name: operating-environment
inputs.desc: Temperature range, humidity, chemical exposure, salt spray, altitude, condensation cycling

inputs.name: rework-requirements
inputs.desc: Frequency and method of field rework or depot repair expected

inputs.name: thermal-management-needs
inputs.desc: Whether the coating will affect component cooling (coating acts as thermal insulator)

inputs.name: regulatory-requirements
inputs.desc: UL, MIL-I-46058C, IPC-CC-830, RoHS, or customer-specific requirements

outputs.name: coating-selection
outputs.desc: Selected coating type (acrylic AR, silicone SR, urethane UR, epoxy ER, parylene XY) with key properties

outputs.name: thickness-specification
outputs.desc: Target thickness range in microns with rationale from insulation resistance and environmental protection requirements

outputs.name: cure-specification
outputs.desc: Cure method (air dry, UV, thermal, room temperature) with time and temperature requirements

outputs.name: compatibility-assessment
outputs.desc: Compatibility with board materials, components, solder mask, and any other coatings or adhesives on the assembly

process: Acrylic (AR): easiest to apply and rework (soluble in IPA or acetone). Good moisture and fungus resistance. Temperature range -65 to +125C. Use for commercial products requiring field rework. Does not withstand chemical solvents in the field environment.

Silicone (SR): widest temperature range (-65 to +200C), excellent moisture resistance, good flexibility for thermal cycling. Difficult to rework (requires specialized solvents or mechanical removal). Use for automotive, aerospace, or any application with wide temperature excursions. Does not provide hard abrasion resistance.

Urethane (UR): excellent chemical and abrasion resistance, good moisture barrier, temperature range -65 to +125C. Difficult to rework (requires hot solvents or burnthrough). Use for harsh chemical environments or where physical durability is needed. Stiff at low temperatures; not ideal for extreme thermal cycling.

Parylene (XY): vapor-deposited, ultra-thin (5-25um), pin-hole-free coverage including under components and sharp edges. Exceptional moisture barrier at minimal thickness. Temperature range -65 to +150C (type C up to 200C). Extremely difficult to rework (requires plasma etching or mechanical removal). Use for medical devices, mil-aero, or any application requiring maximum protection with minimum thickness. Highest cost per board.

Select thickness based on the protection requirement. IPC-CC-830 specifies 25-75um for most chemistries (25-50um for parylene). Thicker coatings provide better insulation resistance and moisture barrier but increase thermal resistance and cost. For most commercial applications, 50um target is sufficient. For high-voltage applications, increase thickness per the insulation resistance vs voltage requirement.

steps.description: Design the masking strategy and apply conformal coating using the method matched to the coating type, board volume, and coverage requirements.

inputs.name: coating-selection
inputs.desc: Selected coating chemistry

inputs.name: thickness-specification
inputs.desc: Target thickness range

inputs.name: board-assembly-drawing
inputs.desc: Assembly drawing showing keep-out areas (connectors, test points, heat sinks, switches, optical sensors)

outputs.name: masking-plan
outputs.desc: Keep-out areas with masking method for each (tape, boots, liquid mask, fixture)

outputs.name: application-method
outputs.desc: Selected application method (spray, selective, dip, brush) with equipment settings

outputs.name: application-procedure
outputs.desc: Step-by-step application procedure including surface preparation, application, and cure

outputs.name: coverage-specification
outputs.desc: Required coverage areas and acceptable exclusion zones defined on a marked-up assembly drawing

process: Identify all areas that must remain uncoated: connectors (mating surfaces), test points (for ICT access), adjustment components (potentiometers, switches), heat sinks (coating insulates), LEDs (coating changes light transmission), sensors (coating affects sensitivity), and any areas requiring post-coating soldering.

Select masking method by area type. Polyimide tape (Kapton) for straight-edge masking of flat areas. Custom boots (silicone or latex) for connectors that need repeated masking. Liquid latex mask (peelable) for irregular shapes. Dedicated masking fixture for high-volume production with many keep-outs.

Select application method. Spray coating: good for medium to high volume, uniform thickness over flat surfaces, requires spray booth. Selective coating (robotic dispensing): programmable path avoids keep-outs without masking, best for high-volume with many keep-outs. Dip coating: uniform coverage including under components, high material usage, suitable for high-reliability where 100% coverage including component undersides is required. Brush: for touch-up and small-batch prototype only.

Prepare the board surface before coating. The surface must be clean and dry. Any flux residue, fingerprints, or contamination will reduce coating adhesion. For no-clean solder paste, verify that the flux residue is compatible with the coating chemistry (some coatings do not adhere well to no-clean residues). If required, clean with IPA or aqueous wash and verify cleanliness per IPC-J-STD-001 (ionic contamination < 1.56 ug NaCl eq/cm2).

Apply the coating per the selected method. For spray: maintain 20-30cm nozzle distance, 50% overlap between passes, fan pattern perpendicular to board travel. Apply in 2-3 light coats rather than one heavy coat to avoid runs and bubbles. Between coats, allow flash-off time (30-60 seconds) for solvent evaporation.

steps.description: Verify coating cure completeness and inspect for coverage defects using visual, UV fluorescence, and thickness measurement methods.

inputs.name: cure-specification
inputs.desc: Cure method, time, and temperature

inputs.name: thickness-specification
inputs.desc: Target thickness range

inputs.name: coverage-specification
inputs.desc: Required coverage and exclusion zones

inputs.name: application-method
inputs.desc: Application method used

outputs.name: cure-verification-results
outputs.desc: Confirmation of complete cure by the specified method (tack-free test, hardness test, FTIR)

outputs.name: coverage-inspection-results
outputs.desc: Visual and UV fluorescence inspection results documenting coverage completeness

outputs.name: thickness-measurement-results
outputs.desc: Measured thickness at specified locations compared to the specification

outputs.name: coating-defect-log
outputs.desc: Any coating defects found (bubbles, pinholes, thin spots, contamination under coating) with disposition

process: Cure the coating per the specification. Air-dry acrylics: 24 hours at room temperature or 30 minutes at 80C for accelerated cure. UV-cure coatings: exposure per the vendor specification (intensity and time), noting that shadow areas under components do not receive UV and may require a secondary thermal or moisture cure. Thermal cure urethanes: 60-90 minutes at 80-100C. Verify oven temperature uniformity.

Verify cure completeness. The simplest test is the tack-free test: press a clean finger on the coating and verify no material transfers. For quantitative verification, use a Shore A durometer hardness measurement compared to the vendor's fully-cured specification. For critical applications, use FTIR spectroscopy to verify the cure chemistry is complete (no unreacted functional groups).

Inspect coverage using UV fluorescence. Most conformal coatings contain UV-fluorescent additives. Under a UV lamp (365nm wavelength), coated areas fluoresce blue-green and uncoated areas appear dark. Inspect 100% of the board surface under UV to verify complete coverage in required areas and no coating in keep-out areas. Document any discrepancies.

Measure thickness at specified locations. Use an eddy current thickness gauge (for conductive substrates) or a magnetic thickness gauge. Measure at minimum 3 locations per board: one on a flat area, one on a component lead, and one on a board edge. All measurements must fall within the specified range. Thickness less than the minimum indicates insufficient protection; thickness greater than the maximum may indicate processing issues.

Inspect for coating defects. Bubbles: trapped air or solvent, caused by too-thick application or insufficient flash-off time. Pinholes: tiny holes that breach the coating, caused by surface contamination or outgassing from the substrate. Dewetting: coating pulling away from the surface, caused by contamination or incompatible substrate. Each defect type has a specific corrective action.

steps.description: Develop rework procedures for conformal-coated assemblies including coating removal methods, component replacement, and re-coating techniques.

inputs.name: coating-selection
inputs.desc: Coating type determining removal method

inputs.name: application-method
inputs.desc: Original application method for re-coating consistency

inputs.name: rework-requirements
inputs.desc: Types of rework expected (component replacement, jumper wires, ECO modifications)

outputs.desc: Step-by-step coating removal method for each coating type with chemical and thermal options

outputs.name: re-coating-procedure
outputs.desc: Method to re-coat after rework, matching the original coating quality

outputs.name: rework-inspection-criteria
outputs.desc: Inspection requirements after rework to verify coating integrity

outputs.name: rework-limitation-list
outputs.desc: Any rework operations that are not feasible or not recommended for the selected coating type

process: Acrylic removal: apply IPA or a dedicated acrylic stripper to the target area using a brush or swab. Allow the solvent to soften the coating (1-2 minutes). Carefully peel or scrape the softened coating from the work area. Repeat as needed until the copper/solder surface is exposed. Acrylics are the easiest coating to rework.

Urethane removal: requires hot solvent (dedicated urethane stripper at 50-60C) or mechanical removal (scraping with a non-metallic tool to avoid board damage). Urethane does not dissolve easily at room temperature. Allow extended soak time (5-10 minutes). Be aware of the chemical hazards of hot strippers and ensure adequate ventilation.

Silicone removal: use a dedicated silicone stripper or a micro-abrasive tool. Silicone is flexible and does not respond well to solvents. Mechanical removal (cutting, peeling) works for thick applications. For thin silicone coatings, a solvent soak followed by gentle scraping is more practical.

Parylene removal: cannot be chemically dissolved at room temperature. Options are: oxygen plasma etching (requires plasma equipment), micro-abrasive blasting (localized removal), or thermal removal (heating above decomposition temperature, but this risks component damage). Parylene rework is inherently difficult and should be avoided by design (ensure the design is correct before parylene application).

After component replacement, re-coat the reworked area. For spray-applied coatings, use a touch-up spray or brush application. Feather the new coating into the existing coating with at least 5mm overlap to avoid a discontinuous boundary. Cure the touch-up per the original cure specification. Inspect under UV to verify continuous fluorescence across the rework boundary.

description: Plan and execute a transition from tin-lead to lead-free soldering across the manufacturing process, addressing alloy selection, process requalification, component compatibility, reliability validation, and regulatory compliance.

steps.description: Evaluate lead-free solder alloy candidates for the specific product application, comparing thermal, mechanical, and manufacturing properties against tin-lead baseline.

inputs.name: product-application
inputs.desc: End-use environment (consumer, automotive, industrial, aerospace, medical) affecting alloy selection

inputs.name: current-snpb-process
inputs.desc: Current tin-lead process parameters as the baseline for comparison

inputs.name: component-compatibility
inputs.desc: Component terminal finish and maximum temperature ratings

inputs.name: board-laminate
inputs.desc: Board material Tg and Td (decomposition temperature) limiting peak reflow temperature

outputs.name: alloy-comparison-matrix
outputs.desc: Side-by-side comparison of SAC305, SAC105, SN100C, and specialty alloys on all relevant properties

outputs.name: selected-alloy
outputs.desc: Recommended lead-free alloy with rationale from the comparison matrix

outputs.name: process-impact-assessment
outputs.desc: Changes required to the existing process for the selected alloy (temperatures, flux, stencil, profile)

outputs.name: component-requalification-list
outputs.desc: Components requiring requalification for the higher reflow temperature

process: SAC305 (Sn96.5/Ag3.0/Cu0.5): industry standard lead-free alloy. Liquidus 217-220C. Good mechanical strength, good thermal fatigue resistance. Higher cost due to silver content. Slightly higher melting point than SnPb (183C) requires process changes. Recommended for general-purpose applications.

SAC105 (Sn98.5/Ag1.0/Cu0.5): lower cost (less silver), lower mechanical strength than SAC305 but better ductility. Better drop shock performance (more compliant joints). Recommended for portable electronics where drop is the primary failure mode.

SN100C (Sn/Cu0.7/Ni0.05/Ge): silver-free, lowest cost lead-free option. Liquidus 227C (slightly higher than SAC). Good wetting with the nickel and germanium additions. Recommended for wave soldering where the solder pot cost of SAC is prohibitive.

Assess peak reflow temperature impact. SAC305 requires 235-245C peak vs 210-225C for SnPb. This 20-30C increase affects: component survival (check maximum temperature ratings; many components are rated to 260C for 10 seconds per J-STD-020), board laminate (standard FR-4 with Tg 130C and Td 300C is adequate; low-Tg materials may delaminate), and process energy cost.

Identify components requiring requalification. Any component rated below 260C peak temperature for 10 seconds must be evaluated. Electrolytic capacitors, some connectors with plastic housings, and components with internal solder joints that may reflow at the higher temperature are primary concerns. Contact component vendors for lead-free compatibility declarations.

steps.description: Requalify each assembly process stage for lead-free soldering, adjusting parameters to account for the higher liquidus temperature and different wetting characteristics.

inputs.name: selected-alloy
inputs.desc: Selected lead-free alloy and its properties

inputs.name: process-impact-assessment
inputs.desc: Process changes required for the transition

inputs.name: current-snpb-process
inputs.desc: Current tin-lead process parameters

outputs.name: lead-free-process-parameters
outputs.desc: Qualified process parameters for each assembly stage with the lead-free alloy

outputs.name: equipment-modifications
outputs.desc: Equipment changes required (higher temperature capability, nitrogen, flux compatibility)

outputs.name: process-capability-comparison
outputs.desc: Cpk comparison between SnPb and lead-free for each critical parameter

outputs.name: requalification-report
outputs.desc: Formal process qualification report for the lead-free conversion

process: Solder paste printing: lead-free paste (SAC305) has different rheology than SnPb paste. Stencil life may be shorter (lead-free flux is more active and degrades faster on the stencil). Re-optimize print parameters: speed, pressure, separation may need adjustment. Verify transfer efficiency with SPI.

Reflow profile: increase peak temperature from 210-225C (SnPb) to 235-245C (SAC305). Time above liquidus must be recalculated for the higher liquidus (217C vs 183C). The process window is narrower: the gap between minimum peak (227C for adequate wetting) and maximum component temperature (260C) is only 33C, compared to 50C+ for SnPb. Nitrogen atmosphere may be required to achieve reliable wetting at the lower end of the peak temperature range.

Wave soldering: increase pot temperature from 245-250C (SnPb) to 255-265C (SAC305). Higher temperature increases copper dissolution rate from board pads and component leads. Monitor copper content in the pot more frequently. Dross formation increases at higher temperature; nitrogen blanket becomes more cost-justified.

Rework: lead-free rework requires higher tip temperatures (370-400C vs 315-350C for SnPb). The higher temperature increases the risk of pad lifting and laminate damage during rework. Rework operators must be retrained on technique and heat management. Consider using a lower-melting-point alloy for rework (such as SnBi) if the product allows it.

Run the full process qualification (capability studies, SPC setup, FAI) with the lead-free parameters. Compare the Cpk values to the SnPb baseline. If Cpk is lower for lead-free, identify the parameter driving the reduction and optimize further. The lead-free process is inherently narrower in process window, so achieving the same Cpk may require tighter equipment control.

steps.description: Manage the transition period where both SnPb and lead-free components and boards coexist in the supply chain and on the production floor.

inputs.name: lead-free-process-parameters
inputs.desc: Qualified lead-free parameters

inputs.name: component-requalification-list
inputs.desc: Components being transitioned to lead-free finish

inputs.name: selected-alloy
inputs.desc: Target lead-free alloy

outputs.name: component-finish-tracking
outputs.desc: System for tracking which components are SnPb-finished vs lead-free-finished in inventory

outputs.name: mixed-assembly-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for handling mixed solder alloy situations (SnPb component on lead-free board and vice versa)

outputs.name: cross-contamination-prevention
outputs.desc: Procedures to prevent SnPb contamination of lead-free processes and materials

outputs.name: transition-timeline
outputs.desc: Phased timeline for completing the full transition from SnPb to lead-free

process: During the transition, the supply chain may deliver components with either SnPb or lead-free terminal finishes. Track component finish in the ERP system. Lead-free components are typically marked with the 'e' or leaf symbol per JEDEC/IPC J-STD-609. Verify incoming component finish by visual inspection (lead-free SAC is typically matte vs shiny SnPb) or by XRF analysis for high-reliability applications.

Define rules for mixed situations. Lead-free (SAC-finished) components soldered with SnPb paste at SnPb temperatures: generally acceptable. The SAC finish dissolves into the SnPb solder and the joint is predominately SnPb. SnPb-finished components soldered with lead-free (SAC) paste at lead-free temperatures: the SnPb finish melts and mixes with SAC, creating a mixed-metallurgy joint. This is acceptable per J-STD-001 but may have different reliability characteristics.

Prevent cross-contamination between SnPb and lead-free production. If using the same equipment for both: purge the solder pot completely when switching (lead contamination in a lead-free pot above 0.1% changes the alloy properties and may violate RoHS). Use separate stencils, separate paste containers, and separate wave solder pallets. Label all lead-free materials and tooling distinctly.

Phase the transition by product line rather than attempting all products simultaneously. Start with new designs (design for lead-free from the start). Transition existing products during planned redesigns. Products with military or medical exemptions may remain on SnPb indefinitely.

Validate the reliability of the lead-free assembly for each product category. The reliability characteristics of SAC are different from SnPb: better thermal fatigue life at wide temperature ranges, worse at narrow ranges with long dwells. Worse drop shock performance for SAC305 vs SnPb. Each product must be validated for its specific use environment.

steps.description: Address tin whisker risk and long-term reliability differences between lead-free and tin-lead solder joints for the product lifetime requirement.

inputs.name: selected-alloy
inputs.desc: Lead-free alloy in use

inputs.name: product-application
inputs.desc: End-use environment and service life

inputs.name: component-finish-tracking
inputs.desc: Terminal finishes on all components

outputs.name: whisker-risk-assessment
outputs.desc: Tin whisker risk classification for each component finish and mitigation measures

outputs.name: reliability-comparison-data
outputs.desc: Thermal cycling, drop, and vibration reliability comparison between lead-free and SnPb for this product

outputs.name: long-term-degradation-model
outputs.desc: Intermetallic growth and aging model for the lead-free joints over the product service life

outputs.name: mitigation-plan
outputs.desc: Specific actions to mitigate any reliability gaps identified in the comparison

process: Assess tin whisker risk. Pure tin finishes on component leads are the primary whisker risk. Whiskers are conductive filaments that grow from tin surfaces under compressive stress, potentially causing shorts. SAC solder alloy joints have low whisker risk because the silver and copper additions relieve internal stress. Component lead finishes of pure tin (matte or bright) on closely spaced leads (<0.5mm pitch) in high-reliability applications require mitigation.

Whisker mitigation options: conformal coating (prevents whisker bridging even if whiskers grow), hot-solder-dipped component leads (replaces pure tin finish with SnPb or SAC), specifying NiPdAu or SnBi component finish (inherently low whisker risk), or component requalification testing per JEDEC JESD201 (environmental stress testing for whisker growth over 3000-4000 hours).

Compare thermal fatigue reliability. SAC305 has approximately 2-3x better thermal fatigue life than SnPb at wide temperature ranges (-40 to +125C) due to its higher creep resistance. At narrow temperature ranges (0 to +60C) with long dwell times (>4 hours), SAC305 may underperform SnPb because the high-temperature dwell allows microstructural coarsening that reduces fatigue resistance.

Compare mechanical shock (drop) reliability. SnPb is generally more ductile and absorbs shock energy better than SAC305. SAC305 BGA joints are susceptible to pad cratering (fracture in the board laminate under the pad) under high-G shock. SAC105 or SnBiAg alloys provide better drop performance than SAC305 if drop is the dominant failure mode.

Model long-term intermetallic compound (IMC) growth. Cu6Sn5 and Cu3Sn IMC layers grow at the solder-copper interface over time, following Arrhenius kinetics: thickness = sqrt(D0 x exp(-Ea/kT) x t), where D0 is the diffusivity constant, Ea is the activation energy, T is temperature, and t is time. For SAC305 on copper at 100C continuous operation, IMC thickness reaches approximately 5-8 microns after 10 years. IMC layers above 10 microns may reduce joint ductility and fatigue resistance.

description: Conduct a process FMEA from process flow diagram through failure mode identification, risk assessment, and control plan development, using the AIAG/VDA PFMEA method for electronics manufacturing.

steps.description: Decompose the manufacturing process flow into discrete steps with function descriptions that serve as the starting point for failure mode identification.

inputs.name: assembly-process-flow
inputs.desc: Step-by-step manufacturing process from incoming material through final test and packaging

inputs.name: bill-of-process
inputs.desc: Equipment, tooling, and materials at each process step

inputs.name: product-requirements
inputs.desc: Customer requirements and specifications that the process must satisfy

outputs.name: process-step-list
outputs.desc: Each process step with its function described as: verb + object + specification (e.g., 'print solder paste within +/-50% volume tolerance')

outputs.name: step-function-mapping
outputs.desc: Each step's function mapped to the product requirement it fulfills

outputs.name: process-boundaries
outputs.desc: Clear definition of PFMEA scope: starting point, ending point, and interfaces with other processes

process: Start with the process flow diagram. Each box in the flow is a process step. Include all steps: receiving inspection, storage, kitting, print, placement, reflow, AOI, X-ray, manual insertion, wave solder, cleaning, coating, ICT, functional test, final inspection, packaging.

For each step, write the function in the form: verb + object + specification. Examples: 'Apply solder paste to PCB pads with volume within +/-30% of nominal.' 'Place components at specified locations with offset < 50% of pad width.' 'Reflow solder joints with peak temperature 235-245C and TAL 40-90 seconds.' The function must be specific enough that a failure to achieve it is clearly identifiable.

Map each function to the product requirement it serves. 'Apply solder paste within specification' serves the requirement of 'solder joints meet IPC-A-610 Class 2 criteria.' This mapping ensures that every product requirement has at least one process step responsible for achieving it. Gaps indicate missing process steps.

Define the PFMEA scope boundaries. The PFMEA covers from the first manufacturing step (incoming materials receiving) to the last step (packaged product ready for shipment). It does not cover design issues (those belong in the DFMEA) or field use issues. Interface points with other processes (e.g., incoming material from the board fabricator, outgoing product to the customer's receiving dock) are boundary conditions.

steps.description: Systematically identify potential failure modes for each process step by asking how the step function could fail, what effect the failure has on the product, and what causes each failure mode.

inputs.name: process-step-list
inputs.desc: Process steps with functions

inputs.name: step-function-mapping
inputs.desc: Requirements mapping

inputs.name: historical-defect-data
inputs.desc: Past defect data informing known failure modes

outputs.name: failure-mode-table
outputs.desc: Each failure mode with its process step, function, effect on product, and potential causes

outputs.name: effect-severity-mapping
outputs.desc: Each effect classified by severity to the end customer

outputs.name: cause-mechanism-mapping
outputs.desc: Each cause linked to the physical or process mechanism that produces the failure mode

process: For each process step, ask: 'In what ways can this step fail to achieve its function?' The failure mode is the opposite of the function. Function: 'Apply paste within +/-30% volume.' Failure modes: paste volume too high, paste volume too low, paste offset from pad, paste bridging adjacent pads, no paste on pad, paste on solder mask.

For each failure mode, determine the effect on the end customer. Paste volume too low -> insufficient solder joint -> potential open circuit in the field -> product failure. The effect chain traces from the immediate process defect to the final customer impact. The severity rating will be based on the worst reasonable customer effect.

For each failure mode, identify the potential causes. A single failure mode may have multiple causes. Paste volume too low may be caused by: clogged stencil aperture, paste not replenished on stencil, squeegee speed too fast, stencil worn (aperture enlarged), paste viscosity too high (cold paste). Each cause is a separate line in the PFMEA because each has its own prevention and detection controls.

Use historical defect data to inform the failure mode list but do not limit it to past failures. Ask 'what else could go wrong?' for each step. Include failure modes from similar products, industry literature (IPC defect databases), and process engineering experience. The goal is to be thorough; a failure mode not identified in the PFMEA cannot be prevented.

Classify each cause by its mechanism. Equipment-related (printer malfunction, oven temperature drift), material-related (paste lot variation, component finish issue), method-related (inadequate procedure, wrong recipe loaded), operator-related (setup error, loading error), environmental (temperature, humidity), measurement-related (inspection system miscalibrated). The mechanism guides the type of control needed.

steps.description: Rate each failure mode for severity, occurrence, and detection using process-specific rating scales anchored to electronics manufacturing evidence.

inputs.name: failure-mode-table
inputs.desc: Complete failure mode, effect, and cause listing

inputs.name: effect-severity-mapping
inputs.desc: Customer effect for severity rating

inputs.name: production-data
inputs.desc: Defect rate data for occurrence estimation

inputs.name: inspection-strategy-design
inputs.desc: Current detection methods and their capabilities

outputs.name: rated-fmea-table
outputs.desc: FMEA table with severity, occurrence, and detection ratings for each cause

outputs.name: action-priority-ranking
outputs.desc: Causes ranked by action priority (AIAG/VDA high/medium/low) or by RPN for prioritization

outputs.name: high-priority-items
outputs.desc: Failure modes requiring immediate action based on severity threshold or action priority

process: Rate Severity (S) on a 1-10 scale anchored to electronics manufacturing effects. S=10: safety or regulatory non-compliance (product catches fire, regulatory recall). S=9: product fails in the field with no warning. S=8: product function degraded; customer dissatisfied. S=7: product appearance defect visible to customer. S=5-6: defect caught at customer incoming inspection. S=3-4: defect caught at our final test. S=1-2: defect caught at in-process inspection with minimal rework. Severity is based on the worst effect; it cannot be reduced by detection.

Rate Occurrence (O) on a 1-10 scale anchored to process defect rates. O=10: defect rate > 100,000 ppm (10% or higher). O=8: 10,000-50,000 ppm (1-5%). O=6: 1,000-5,000 ppm (0.1-0.5%). O=4: 100-500 ppm (0.01-0.05%). O=2: 1-10 ppm (< 0.001%). O=1: defect is eliminated by design (physically impossible). Use actual defect data where available; estimate from similar processes where not.

Rate Detection (D) on a 1-10 scale anchored to inspection capability. D=10: no inspection or detection method for this failure mode. D=9: visual inspection only (operator-dependent, variable). D=7: manual measurement (caliper, multimeter). D=5: automated inspection (AOI, SPI) with demonstrated detection rate > 95%. D=3: automated inspection with detection rate > 99%. D=1: failure mode is physically prevented by mistake-proofing (poka-yoke) such that it cannot occur.

The AIAG/VDA FMEA method (4th edition, 2019) replaces RPN with an Action Priority (AP) matrix that separately considers S, O, and D combinations. High priority: any item with S >= 9 and O >= 4, or S >= 9 and D >= 7. Medium priority: moderate risk combinations. Low priority: adequately controlled. Use AP instead of RPN because RPN can rank a S=3/O=5/D=10 (AP:Low, no safety risk) equally with S=10/O=3/D=5 (AP:High, safety concern).

Identify all items with AP=High for immediate action. These are the items where the combination of severity, occurrence, and detection creates unacceptable risk. Also flag any item with severity of 9 or 10 regardless of occurrence and detection, because the consequence of escape is too severe to accept any detection gap.

steps.description: Translate the PFMEA action priorities into a production control plan that links each critical process parameter to its measurement method, frequency, control limit, and reaction plan.

inputs.name: rated-fmea-table
inputs.desc: Complete rated PFMEA

inputs.name: high-priority-items
inputs.desc: Items requiring immediate action

inputs.name: action-priority-ranking
inputs.desc: Full ranked list for control plan coverage

outputs.name: control-plan-document
outputs.desc: Production control plan with one row per controlled characteristic, following AIAG format

outputs.name: prevention-controls
outputs.desc: Prevention measures for each high-priority item (mistake-proofing, parameter control, maintenance schedules)

outputs.name: detection-controls
outputs.desc: Detection measures for each item where prevention alone is insufficient (inspection, test, SPC)

outputs.name: reaction-procedures
outputs.desc: Out-of-control response procedures for each controlled parameter

process: For each PFMEA item rated High priority, define a prevention control (reduces occurrence) and/or a detection control (improves detection). Prevention is always preferred over detection. Example: for 'clogged stencil aperture causing low paste volume,' the prevention control is 'scheduled under-stencil cleaning every 3 prints' and the detection control is '100% SPI with volume alarm at -30% of nominal.'

Build the control plan document. Each row contains: process step, controlled characteristic (the specific thing being monitored), specification (the acceptance criteria), measurement method (the tool and technique), sample size and frequency, control method (SPC chart type, go/no-go gauge, automated alarm), and reaction plan (what to do when the limit is exceeded).

Ensure flow-down from PFMEA to control plan to work instruction. Every high-priority PFMEA item must appear in the control plan. Every control plan measurement must appear in the operator work instruction with specific instructions for how to perform the measurement and what to do with the result.

For safety-related items (Severity 9 or 10), the control plan must include mistake-proofing (poka-yoke) wherever feasible. Example: component polarity error on a safety-critical circuit -> poka-yoke: the pick-and-place program verifies component polarity using vision; a wrong-polarity component is rejected before placement. The detection method for poka-yoke is verification that the mistake-proofing device is functioning correctly.

Review the control plan with the production team before release. The people who will execute the plan must understand it, agree that it is achievable, and have the training and equipment to perform each measurement. A control plan that exists on paper but is not executed on the floor provides no protection.

Schedule regular PFMEA and control plan reviews. The PFMEA is a living document. Review whenever: a new defect type is discovered, a process change is made, a customer complaint is received, or at a minimum annual interval. Update the ratings based on current data and adjust the control plan accordingly.
